AI Product Manager

  • Write PRDs for LLM/RAG/agent features with evals and guardrails

Data / AI Analyst

GenAI / AI Automation Specialist

Career path · 12 classes · basic to advanced

AI Engineer: The Complete Path

An AI engineer builds, ships and runs AI-powered software: calling and customising models, connecting them to data and tools, testing quality, deploying reliably, keeping cost, safety and security under control, and improving the system with real usage.

Basic · Class 1

The AI engineer role and the lifecycle

Know what the job is, how it differs from neighbouring roles, and the lifecycle you'll work in.

RoleMainly does
AI engineerBuilds products on top of models: LLM apps, RAG, agents, evals, deployment
ML engineerTrains and serves custom models, feature pipelines, MLOps
Data scientistAnalysis, experiments, modelling, insights
Data engineerPipelines, warehouses, data quality
Software engineerApplication backend/frontend, systems
Forward-deployed engineerBuilds AI solutions at customer sites
Prompt / context engineerDesigns instructions and context; a skill inside AI engineering

A typical week

  • Clarify a use case with the PM; define success metrics and an eval set.
  • Prototype with a model API; build retrieval and tools; iterate on failures.
  • Write services, tests and CI; deploy; watch dashboards for quality, cost and latency.
  • Review incidents, update evals, tune prompts, retrieval and models; document decisions.

Learn it here: How LLMs work · Building and shipping a GenAI app · Forward Deployed Engineer guide

Key takeaways
  • AI engineering = software engineering + models + evals + operations.
  • Work in a loop: define, build, evaluate, deploy, improve.
  • Neighbouring roles overlap; know the boundaries.
Practice: Write a one-page 'day in the life' of an AI engineer for a support-copilot project, with 5 tasks.
Basic · Class 2

Foundations: Python, software engineering, Git, APIs, Linux

Build the engineering base that every AI system sits on.

SkillBe able to…
PythonWrite functions/classes, use virtualenvs and pip/uv, read/write files and JSON, handle errors, use async for many API calls
Testingpytest, fixtures, mocking API calls, writing tests before you ship
GitBranch, commit, rebase/merge, open pull requests, resolve conflicts
HTTP/APIsCall REST APIs, handle auth, rate limits, retries with backoff, webhooks
SQL & dataJoins, aggregates, window functions, indexes; pandas for analysis
TerminalNavigate, grep, curl, environment variables, secrets handling

Starter script: call a model API with retries

import os, time, requests
def call(prompt, tries=3):
    for i in range(tries):
        r = requests.post(URL, headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['API_KEY']}"},
                          json={"model": MODEL, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]}, timeout=60)
        if r.status_code == 200: return r.json()
        if r.status_code in (429, 500, 502, 503): time.sleep(2 ** i); continue
        r.raise_for_status()
    raise RuntimeError("model API unavailable")

Learn it here: Python track (29 lessons) · SQL track · APIs without code · APIs, JSON and web scraping · Python and SQL

Key takeaways
  • Python + testing + Git + HTTP are non-negotiable.
  • Handle rate limits and retries from day one.
  • Never put secrets in code.
Practice: Build a small CLI that calls a model API, handles errors with retries and has 3 pytest tests.

AreaKnow

Practice: Train and evaluate a classifier on a Kaggle dataset with proper train/validation/test splits and 3 metrics.
Intermediate · Class 4

LLM engineering: model APIs, prompts, structured output, cost and latency

Build reliable features on top of model APIs.

  • Providers: Anthropic Claude, OpenAI, Google Gemini, plus open models (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek) via Hugging Face, Ollama, vLLM, Groq, Together.
  • Key parameters: system prompt, temperature/sampling (where supported), max tokens, stop sequences, streaming, tool definitions, structured outputs/JSON schema.
  • Tokens & context: price per input/output token, context window limits, prompt caching, batching for cost.
  • Reliability: timeouts, retries with backoff, provider fallbacks, circuit breakers, idempotency.
  • Quality: few-shot examples, chain-of-thought where useful, self-checks, guardrails.
  • Cost & latency: route simple tasks to small models, cache, trim context, stream for perceived speed. Track cost per successful task.
cost per request = input_tokens × price_in + output_tokens × price_out
latency budget   = retrieval + model + tools + post-processing   (set a target for each)

Learn it here: Prompt engineering in depth · Calling LLM APIs from Python · Prompt & Context Engineering course · Pricing & Monetising AI

Key takeaways
  • Treat the model as an unreliable remote service: validate, retry, fall back.
  • Track tokens, cost and latency on every call.
  • Structured outputs make LLMs usable in code.
Practice: Build a function that returns validated JSON from an LLM, with retries, a fallback model and a cost log.
Intermediate · Class 5

RAG, embeddings and vector databases

Build search and question-answering over private data, and measure it.

PartOptions and decisions
IngestionParsers for PDF/HTML/Docs, OCR for scans, incremental refresh, access control metadata
ChunkingBy headings/sections, 300–800 tokens, overlap, keep tables intact
EmbeddingsOpenAI, Cohere, Voyage, Gemini, open models (bge, e5); multilingual for Hindi
Vector storespgvector (Postgres), Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus, Chroma, FAISS, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch
RetrievalHybrid (BM25 + vectors), metadata filters, query rewriting, rerankers (Cohere Rerank, cross-encoders), MMR
AdvancedGraphRAG, agentic RAG, multi-vector, parent-document retrieval, caching
EvaluationRecall@k, MRR, faithfulness, answer relevance (see AI Evals)

Learn it here: Embeddings and vector search · RAG: build, evaluate, improve · AI Evals · AI Second Brain

Key takeaways
  • Retrieval quality limits answer quality.
  • Hybrid search + reranking beat vectors alone.
  • Measure retrieval and generation separately.
Practice: Build a RAG Q&A over 20 PDFs with citations; report recall@3 and faithfulness on 30 questions.
Intermediate · Class 6

Agents, tool use and MCP

Build agents that call tools, with control and observability.

  • Tool/function calling: describe tools with JSON schemas; the model returns structured calls; your code executes and returns results.
  • MCP (Model Context Protocol): standard way to expose tools and data to AI assistants; build MCP servers for your product; use existing ones (GitHub, Slack, Playwright, databases).
  • Frameworks: LangGraph, LangChain, LlamaIndex, OpenAI Agents SDK, Claude Agent SDK, CrewAI, AutoGen, Pydantic AI; or plain code (often the best start).
  • Patterns: chaining, routing, parallel, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer (see Orchestration course).
  • Memory: short-term (conversation), long-term (vector store/db), summaries, user profile.
  • Control: step/cost limits, approvals for risky tools, sandboxing code execution, tracing every run.
  • Computer & browser use: Playwright MCP, Browser Use (see Web Automation course).

Learn it here: Tool use and function calling · AI agents and agentic AI · MCP · Claude Code tutorial · Agent Orchestration · Web Automation

Key takeaways
  • Agents = LLM + tools + loop + guardrails.
  • Start with simple workflows; add autonomy when evals justify it.
  • MCP standardises tool access.
Practice: Build an agent with 3 tools (search, calculator, database lookup) with a step limit and full trace logging.
Advanced · Class 7

Customising models: fine-tuning, distillation and open-source models

Decide when to fine-tune, and how, and when not to.

MethodWhen
Better prompts and examplesAlways first
RAGKnowledge changes or is private; need citations
Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)Consistent style/format, domain behaviour, shorter prompts, cost reduction
LoRA / QLoRAParameter-efficient tuning of open models on one GPU
Preference tuning (DPO, RLHF concepts)Align outputs with human preferences
DistillationTeach a small, cheap model from a large one's outputs

Fine-tuning workflow

  1. Collect 500–5,000 high-quality examples (inputs and ideal outputs); clean and split train/validation/test.
  2. Baseline with prompting; define eval metrics first.
  3. Fine-tune (provider fine-tuning APIs, or Hugging Face Transformers, PEFT, TRL, Unsloth, Axolotl).
  4. Evaluate against the baseline on held-out data; check regressions and safety.
  5. Deploy (vLLM, TGI, Ollama, or provider-hosted); monitor drift; retrain on new data.

Learn it here: Customising models: prompting vs RAG vs fine-tuning, LoRA · ML Products for PMs

Key takeaways
  • Prompting → RAG → fine-tuning, in that order.
  • Data quality beats data quantity.
  • Always compare with a prompting baseline.
Practice: Plan (data, metric, baseline, hardware, evaluation) a LoRA fine-tune for classifying support tickets.
Advanced · Class 8

Evals, observability, guardrails and red-teaming

Make quality measurable and keep it that way.

  • Evals: golden dataset, code and LLM-judge graders, human review, regression suite in CI (see AI Evals course).
  • Observability: trace every request (prompt, retrieved docs, tool calls, tokens, cost, latency); tools: Langfuse, LangSmith, Arize Phoenix, Braintrust, OpenTelemetry.
  • Guardrails: input checks (PII, injection), output checks (schema, toxicity, policy), allow-lists for tools, rate limits; libraries such as Guardrails AI, NeMo Guardrails, Llama Guard, provider moderation APIs.
  • Red-teaming: jailbreaks, prompt injection, data exfiltration, harmful content, bias tests; add each finding to the eval set.
  • Online quality: sample live traffic, judge scores, user feedback, A/B tests.

Learn it here: Evaluating LLM applications and guardrails · AI Evals for PMs · AI Governance

Key takeaways
  • No eval, no launch.
  • Trace everything to debug fast.
  • Guardrails are layers, not a single filter.
Practice: Add tracing and a 50-case regression eval to your RAG app and run it in CI.

Advanced · Class 10

Data engineering for AI, security and governance

Feed AI systems good data and keep them safe and compliant.

Data for AI

  • Pipelines (Airflow, Prefect, dbt) that clean, deduplicate and refresh documents and vector indexes.
  • Data quality checks, lineage, versioned datasets; labelling workflows (Label Studio, human review).
  • Synthetic data with review; privacy: mask PII before it reaches prompts, logs or training.

Security (OWASP Top 10 for LLM apps)

RiskControl
Prompt injection (direct and from documents/web)Treat content as data; separate instructions; restrict tool permissions; approvals
Sensitive data leakageAccess control in retrieval, redaction, no secrets in prompts, tenant isolation
Insecure output handlingValidate/escape model output; never run model-written code unsandboxed
Excessive agencyLeast privilege tools, spend/step limits, human approval
Supply chain (models, packages)Pin versions, scan dependencies, trusted model sources
Denial of walletRate limits, quotas, budgets

Governance

DPDP Act consent and minimisation, EU AI Act risk tiers, audit logs, system cards, incident response (see AI Governance course).

Learn it here: AI Governance & Responsible AI · Data modelling · Web Automation (secure webhooks)

Key takeaways
  • Good data pipelines keep RAG fresh and safe.
  • Know the OWASP LLM risks and their controls.
  • Least privilege for every agent tool.
Practice: Write a threat model for an AI support agent that can issue refunds.
Advanced · Class 11

System design for AI products and working with the team

Design end-to-end AI systems and collaborate across roles.

How to answer an AI system-design question

  1. Clarify users, scale, languages, latency and quality targets, risks.
  2. Sketch the architecture (above) and the data flow.
  3. Pick approaches with trade-offs: prompting vs RAG vs fine-tune; one model vs routing; sync vs async.
  4. Cover evals, safety, observability, cost and failure handling.
  5. Discuss rollout: shadow, canary, A/B, human fallback.

Common designs to practise

  • Customer-support copilot (RAG + tools + handoff)
  • Document processing pipeline (OCR → extraction → validation → human review)
  • Voice agent for appointments (STT → LLM → TTS, barge-in, latency)
  • Code assistant (indexing, context selection, sandbox, tests)
  • Internal knowledge search with permissions
  • Recommendation or search ranking with LLM reranking

Working with PMs, designers and data teams

  • Turn PRDs into eval sets and acceptance criteria; push back with data on feasibility and cost.
  • Demo early with real outputs including failures; document assumptions and limits.
  • Be on-call for AI quality: incident reviews, postmortems, new tests.

Learn it here: AI Product Strategy · Designing AI Experiences · Platform & API PM

Key takeaways
  • Always state trade-offs and failure handling.
  • Evals, safety and cost belong in every design.
  • Great AI engineers translate between product and models.
Practice: Design a document-processing AI system for insurance claims and present it in 10 minutes.

Interview prep

12 interview questions with answers

What does an AI engineer do?

Builds, evaluates, deploys and operates AI-powered software: model APIs, RAG, agents and tools, evals, guardrails, cloud deployment and monitoring, with attention to cost, latency and safety.

AI engineer vs ML engineer?

AI engineers mostly build products on existing models (prompts, RAG, agents, evals); ML engineers train and serve custom models and run ML pipelines. The roles overlap.

How would you design a RAG system?

Ingest and chunk documents with metadata, embed, store in a vector DB, retrieve with hybrid search and reranking, generate with citations, enforce access control, evaluate retrieval and faithfulness, monitor and refresh.

When do you fine-tune?

After prompting and RAG fall short: for consistent style or format, narrow tasks, or to lower cost with a smaller model; compare to a prompting baseline on held-out data.

How do you evaluate an LLM application?

Golden dataset with slices, code and LLM-judge graders calibrated to humans, regression tests in CI, online metrics and sampled judging.

How do you reduce hallucinations?

Ground answers in retrieved sources, require citations and 'not found', use structured outputs, add verification steps and evals, and escalate low-confidence cases.

How do you control cost and latency?

Route to smaller models, cache, trim context, stream, batch, set budgets, and track cost per successful task.

What are the main security risks of LLM apps?

Prompt injection, data leakage, insecure output handling, excessive agency, supply chain and denial of wallet; mitigate with least privilege, validation, sandboxing, approvals and rate limits.

Explain MCP.

The Model Context Protocol standardises how AI assistants connect to tools and data; you can build MCP servers to expose your product and use existing ones.

Walk through deploying an AI service.

FastAPI service in Docker, CI with tests and evals, deploy to cloud, gateway for auth/limits/routing, tracing and alerts, canary rollout and rollback.

How do you handle a quality regression in production?

Check traces, compare against the eval set, identify cause (prompt, retrieval, model update, data drift), roll back, fix, add a regression test.

What projects would you show in a portfolio?

A cited RAG app, an agent with tracing, an eval harness in CI, a deployed service with monitoring, and a fine-tune vs prompt comparison.

Lovable: from idea to a working app (no code)

Build and publish an app with Lovable, including a database, login and your own domain.

Step by step

  1. Sign in at lovable.dev → new project → describe the app: users, pages, key actions, style ("A booking app for a Pune yoga studio: home, classes, book a slot, my bookings; calm green style").
  2. Review the first version; ask for changes one at a time ("Add a pricing page with 3 plans", "Make the header sticky").
  3. Connect Supabase for a database and user login; ask Lovable to create the tables (classes, bookings) and sign-up.
  4. Connect GitHub to keep the code (you or a developer can continue in Claude Code or Codex).
  5. Publish, then connect a custom domain in project settings and add the DNS records it shows at your domain provider.

Tips

  • Write a mini-PRD first (pages, data, roles); paste it as the first prompt.
  • Use screenshots or Figma links as references.
  • Never put secret keys in the front end; use the backend's secure settings.

More: PM handbook Module 16: Lovable basic to advanced.

Interview prep

8 interview questions with answers

Which AI tool would you use to prototype an app quickly?

A no-code builder like Lovable (or Bolt/v0/Replit) for a clickable, working prototype; then move to a coding agent for production.

Claude Code vs Lovable?

Lovable is a no-code app builder in the browser; Claude Code is a coding agent that edits real code in your repo, runs commands and deploys, giving full ownership and flexibility.

How would you build a website as a PM?

Plan pages and CTA, generate with Lovable or a coding agent, add pages and forms, analytics and SEO, push to GitHub, deploy on Cloudflare Pages/Netlify, connect a custom domain.

How do you connect a website form to your tools?

Use an automation (Zapier/Make/n8n) or a webhook: form → Sheet → AI summary → Slack/CRM.

What are Custom GPTs and Gems?

Reusable assistants with your instructions and files in ChatGPT (GPTs) and Gemini (Gems).

How do you keep API keys safe?

Store them only in server or hosting secret settings, never in front-end code or prompts; use limits and rotate keys.

When use NotebookLM?

When answers must come from your own sources with citations: research, study, interview synthesis.

How do PMs use coding agents responsibly?

Branches and reviews, project rules files, tests, no secrets in code, and human approval before merging and deploying.

Basic · Class 2

Webhooks explained (with real examples)

Understand webhooks and receive your first one.

A webhook is an automatic message one app sends to a URL you give it when an event happens. Instead of asking "any new payments?" every minute (polling), the provider pushes the news to you instantly.

Common webhooks

ProviderExample events
Razorpay / Stripepayment.captured, refund.processed, subscription.charged
GitHubpush, pull_request, issues
Typeform / Google Forms (via tools)new response
Shopify / WooCommerceorders/create, orders/paid
Slack / WhatsApp Businessmessage received
Calendlyinvitee.created

Example payload

POST https://yourapp.com/webhooks/razorpay
{ "event": "payment.captured",
  "payload": { "payment": { "entity": { "id": "pay_29QQoUBi66xm2f", "amount": 49900,
     "currency": "INR", "email": "riya@example.com", "status": "captured" } } } }

Try it in 5 minutes (no code)

  1. Open a free webhook tester (e.g. webhook.site) and copy your unique URL.
  2. Paste it as the webhook URL in a test tool (a form tool, GitHub repo settings → Webhooks, or Razorpay test mode).
  3. Trigger the event (submit the form, push a commit) and watch the request arrive with its headers and JSON.
Key takeaways
  • Webhooks push events to you in real time.
  • The body is usually JSON describing the event.
  • Test with a webhook inspector before writing code.
Practice: Receive a real webhook from GitHub or a form tool in a webhook tester and identify the event name and key fields.
Intermediate · Class 3

Building reliable webhook receivers

Verify, process and retry webhooks safely in production.

Six rules for production webhooks

  1. Verify the signature (HMAC) so only the real provider can call you.
  2. Respond fast (200 OK within a few seconds); do heavy work in a queue.
  3. Be idempotent: providers retry, so the same event may arrive twice; store event IDs and skip duplicates.
  4. Handle retries and order: events can arrive late or out of order; check current state.
  5. Log everything: raw payload, headers, result; keep a replay option.
  6. Secrets in environment settings, never in code.

Signature check (Node.js / Cloudflare-style function)

import crypto from "node:crypto";
export async function onRequestPost({ request, env }) {
  const body = await request.text();                       // raw body, before JSON parsing
  const sig = request.headers.get("x-razorpay-signature") || "";
  const expected = crypto.createHmac("sha256", env.RAZORPAY_WEBHOOK_SECRET).update(body).digest("hex");
  if (sig.length !== expected.length ||
      !crypto.timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(sig), Buffer.from(expected)))
    return new Response("invalid signature", { status: 401 });
  const event = JSON.parse(body);
  // idempotency: skip if this event id was already processed (check your DB/KV)
  // enqueue the work, then reply quickly
  return new Response("ok");
}

Each provider documents its own header name and signing method; follow its official guide.

Local testing

Expose your laptop with a tunnel (ngrok, Cloudflare Tunnel) or use the provider's CLI to forward test events; replay saved payloads in tests.

Key takeaways
  • Verify signatures, respond fast, be idempotent.
  • Expect retries and out-of-order events.
  • Log and replay for debugging.
Practice: Write the requirements (or code) for a webhook receiver that marks orders paid, including signature, idempotency and logging.

Choose how and when automations start.

TriggerExampleWhere
Schedule (cron)Every day 9:00 IST: download sales reportn8n Schedule, Zapier Schedule, Make scheduling, GitHub Actions cron, Cloudflare Cron Triggers
Webhook / eventNew payment → send receipt on WhatsAppAny webhook trigger node

App eventNew Gmail with label "lead"Zapier/Make/n8n app triggers

Cron in one minute

minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week
0 9 * * 1-5        → 09:00 every weekday
*/15 * * * *       → every 15 minutes
30 18 1 * *        → 18:30 on the 1st of every month
Note: many servers use UTC; 09:00 IST = 03:30 UTC.
Key takeaways
  • Webhooks for instant, schedules for batches, polling when nothing else exists.
  • Watch time zones in cron (IST vs UTC).
  • Add manual triggers for testing.

Intermediate · Class 5

Playwright for browser automation

Automate any website reliably with Playwright.

Playwright (by Microsoft) controls Chromium, Firefox and WebKit from Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, Java or .NET. It auto-waits for elements, records your clicks as code and replays failures step by step.

Setup and record

pip install playwright && playwright install chromium
playwright codegen https://demo.playwright.dev/todomvc/     # click around; code is written for you

Script: log in, export a report (pattern)

from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright
with sync_playwright() as p:
    browser = p.chromium.launch(headless=True)
    ctx = browser.new_context(storage_state="auth.json")   # reuse a saved, authorised login
    page = ctx.new_page()
    page.goto("https://portal.example.com/reports")
    page.get_by_label("From").fill("2026-10-01")
    page.get_by_role("button", name="Export CSV").click()
    with page.expect_download() as d:
        page.get_by_role("link", name="Download").click()
    d.value.save_as("report.csv")
    browser.close()

Make it robust

  • Locate by role, label, text or test id, not fragile CSS paths.
  • Use storage_state for logins (store securely; never commit it).
  • Turn on tracing; open failures in the trace viewer.
  • Run on a schedule (GitHub Actions cron, n8n Execute Command, a small server) with alerts on failure.
Key takeaways
  • Playwright = fast, reliable, multi-browser automation.
  • codegen writes your first script.
  • Saved login state + traces + schedules make it production-ready.
Practice: Record a 5-step flow with codegen, then add a download and run it headless.
Intermediate · Class 6

Playwright MCP: let Claude and other AI assistants use a browser

Install and use the Playwright MCP server with Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor and VS Code.

The Playwright MCP server (by Microsoft) exposes browser actions as MCP tools: navigate, click, type, select, take a snapshot or screenshot, handle tabs and more. By default the AI reads a structured accessibility snapshot of the page (fast and precise), not just pixels.

Install

# Claude Code (terminal)
claude mcp add playwright npx @playwright/mcp@latest

# Claude Desktop / Cursor / VS Code (MCP config JSON)
{ "mcpServers": { "playwright": { "command": "npx", "args": ["@playwright/mcp@latest"] } } }

Useful options include headless mode, choosing the browser, isolated sessions and a persistent profile; see the official README for the current flags.

Things to ask

  • "Open our staging site, sign up with a test email, and tell me every step where the UI is confusing. Take screenshots."
  • "Go to these 5 competitor pricing pages and make a comparison table with plan, price and limits."
  • "Fill the demo booking form on our site with test data but don't submit; report any validation errors."
  • In Claude Code: "Write Playwright tests for the checkout flow you just explored, then run them."

Why it's popular

  • Works with many MCP clients; real browser, real logins (in a test profile).
  • Great for QA, research, debugging UI, and turning exploration into automated tests.

Safety

  • Use a separate test profile/accounts; never your banking or personal sessions.
  • Allow-list sites; require approval for submit/pay/send.
  • Treat page text as untrusted (prompt injection).
Key takeaways
  • Playwright MCP = AI-driven real browser via MCP tools.
  • One command adds it to Claude Code; JSON config for other clients.
  • Great for QA, research and generating tests; keep it sandboxed.
Practice: Add Playwright MCP to Claude Code or Claude Desktop and ask it to compare 3 pricing pages; then ask it to write a Playwright test for one flow.

Know the alternatives and when each wins.

Choosing: new projects usually pick Playwright (speed, auto-wait, multi-browser, MCP); keep Selenium where it already runs; Cypress if your front-end team prefers it; DevTools MCP when debugging performance with AI.

Key takeaways
  • Playwright is the default for new work.
  • Selenium remains common in enterprises.
  • Pick by team skills and browsers needed.

Advanced · Class 10

Production: security, legality, monitoring, evals and capstone

Run web automations safely and prove they work.

Checklist

  • Secrets in environment settings; rotate keys; least-privilege accounts.
  • Respect site terms and robots.txt, rate-limit, never bypass CAPTCHAs; prefer APIs; follow the DPDP Act for personal data.
  • Approvals before submit/pay/send/delete; allow-listed sites for AI agents.
  • Monitoring: success rate, duration, cost, failures with screenshots/traces; alerts to Slack/email.
  • Evals: 20–50 test tasks with known end states; run after changes (see AI Evals course).

Capstone

Build a "competitor & order watch": (1) a webhook receiver for test payments with signature check and idempotency, (2) a daily cron workflow in n8n, (3) a Playwright script that collects 3 competitor prices, (4) a Playwright MCP session in Claude that explores your own site and writes one automated test, (5) alerts and a run log, (6) a 1-page PRD with an approval matrix. Demo in 5 minutes.

Key takeaways
  • Secure, legal, approved, monitored, evaluated.
  • Every failure leaves a trace and an alert.
  • Ship a capstone you can demo in interviews.
Practice: Complete the capstone and present it.

Interview prep

10 interview questions with answers

What is a webhook?

An HTTP request an app sends to your URL when an event happens, so you get updates instantly instead of polling.

How do you secure a webhook endpoint?

Verify the provider's HMAC signature on the raw body, use HTTPS, keep the secret in environment settings, respond fast, and process idempotently.

Webhook vs polling?

Webhooks push instantly and save calls; polling checks repeatedly and adds delay but works when no webhooks exist.

What is idempotency and why does it matter?

Processing the same event twice has no extra effect; needed because providers retry and may send duplicates.

What is the Playwright MCP?

An MCP server by Microsoft that exposes browser actions (navigate, click, type, snapshot) so AI assistants like Claude can use a real browser.

Playwright vs Selenium?

Playwright: newer, faster, auto-waiting, multi-browser, great tooling and MCP. Selenium: mature standard with broad language and grid support, common in existing enterprise suites.

When would you use an AI browser agent instead of a script?

When pages change often or tasks vary; keep scripts for stable steps and add AI for the messy parts, with evals and approvals.

How do you schedule an automation for 9 am IST on weekdays?

Cron '0 9 * * 1-5' in IST, or '30 3 * * 1-5' if the server runs in UTC.

What risks come with browser automation?

Breaking on UI changes, terms-of-service and legal issues, credential leaks, prompt injection for AI agents, and irreversible actions; mitigate with APIs, sandboxes, approvals and monitoring.

Give a PM use case for Playwright MCP.

Ask Claude to walk the onboarding flow on staging, list UX issues with screenshots, then generate Playwright tests for the happy path.

Basic · Class 1

How Zapier works

Know the building blocks and the pricing logic.

  • Zap: one automation. Trigger: the event that starts it. Action: each step after.
  • Task: each successful action run counts toward your plan's monthly limit; triggers and filtered-out runs don't (check the current pricing page).
  • Connections: sign in once per app (Google, Slack, Gmail, Typeform, HubSpot, Notion…).
  • Test steps: every step has a test that pulls real sample data to map into later steps.

Sign up at zapier.com, open Zaps → Create, and look at the editor: trigger on top, actions below, a Publish switch.

Vocabulary you will meet

TermMeaning
ZapOne automation: a trigger and one or more actions
TriggerThe event that starts the Zap (new row, new form entry, new email)
ActionA step that does something (create row, send message)
Search actionLooks up a record (find customer by email)
TaskA successful action run counted toward your plan (check current rules)
ConnectionA saved login to an app, reusable across Zaps
Zap historyLog of every run with inputs and outputs, used for debugging and replay
Folder and sharingOrganise Zaps and share with teammates
VersionEdits are saved as versions you can compare and restore
Check before you build: app names, plan limits, prices and menu labels change often. Use this lesson for the method and confirm the current screens and limits in the official docs.
Key takeaways
  • Zap = trigger + actions.
  • Tasks drive pricing.
  • Always test each step.
Practice: Sign up and list 5 things in your work that start with 'when X happens…'.
Basic · Class 2

Build your first Zap: form → Sheet → Slack

Follow the steps to automate lead capture.

  1. Trigger: choose Google Forms (or Typeform / Webflow) → New Response → connect account → pick the form → Test trigger.
  2. Action 1: Google Sheets → Create Spreadsheet Row; pick the sheet; map each column (Name, Email, Phone) from the trigger data.
  3. Action 2: Slack → Send Channel Message; text: New lead: {Name} ({Email}, {Phone}).
  4. Action 3 (optional): Gmail → Send Email to the lead: "Thanks {Name}, we'll call you within 24 hours."
  5. Test each step, then click Publish. Submit the form once to see it run in Zap runs (history).

Common mistakes in a first Zap

  • Testing with old data: the sample may differ from live data; add a live test.
  • Mapping the wrong field: check each field in the test output.
  • Duplicates: a trigger firing on updates can create duplicates; add a search step or a unique ID check.
  • No owner: name the Zap, add a description and choose an owner and alert email.
Key takeaways
  • Map fields from earlier steps.
  • Test before publishing.
  • Check Zap runs history.
Practice: Build this Zap and run it with 3 test form entries.

Logic: filters, paths, formatter, delay, lookup

Make Zaps smarter without code.

ToolUseExample
FilterContinue only if…Budget ≥ ₹50,000
PathsBranches (if/else)Hot lead → Slack + call; Cold lead → nurture email
FormatterClean text, dates, numbersCapitalise names, format phone to +91…
DelayWait before the next stepSend follow-up after 2 days
Lookup / FindSearch before creatingFind contact by email; update, else create (no duplicates)
LoopingHandle many itemsCreate a row per order item

Formatter cookbook

TaskFormatter stepExample result
Make names consistentText: Capitalizeravi kumar becomes Ravi Kumar
Get the first nameText: Split TextRavi Kumar becomes Ravi
Clean a phone numberText: Replace / Extract Pattern+91 98765-43210 becomes 9876543210

Key takeaways
  • Filters stop, paths branch.
  • Formatter cleans data.
  • Look up before creating to avoid duplicates.
Practice: Add a filter and a 2-path split to your lead Zap.
Intermediate · Class 4

Webhooks, AI steps and Tables

Connect any app and add AI.

  • Webhooks by Zapier: Catch Hook gives you a URL; your website or Razorpay POSTs JSON to it; use the fields in later steps. POST action sends data out. Test with a webhook tester first.
  • AI steps: add an AI/ChatGPT/Claude step ("Classify this lead as Hot/Warm/Cold and write a 2-line summary") then route on its answer.
  • Tables & Interfaces: store records and build simple forms or approval pages (look for current names in your plan).
  • Reliability: turn on autoreplay/error notifications; use Zap names and folders.

Webhook safety

  • Treat the Catch Hook URL as a secret; rotate it if leaked.
  • Verify a shared secret or signature header if the sender supports it.
  • Return quickly; do heavy work in later steps.
  • Log the payload for debugging, but mask personal data.
Key takeaways
  • Catch Hook = custom trigger.
  • AI step + path = smart routing.
  • Turn on error alerts.
Practice: Send a test webhook from webhook.site into a Zap and route on a field.

Intermediate · Class 7

Working with data: line items, lookups, duplicates and multi-step flows

Handle the tricky data problems that break automations.

  • Line items: orders with many products arrive as lists. Use Looping to process each item, or convert to text for a summary message.
  • Find or create: search for the customer by email; if found, update; otherwise create. This prevents duplicates.
  • Unique IDs: store the source ID in the destination so reruns cannot duplicate records.
  • Missing data: add a Filter that stops the Zap if a required field is empty, and a separate path that alerts someone.
  • Time zones and formats: convert to Asia/Kolkata and a standard format before saving.
  • Rate limits: add Delay steps when sending many API calls or messages.
  • Sub-Zaps / reusable parts: where available, keep common logic (for example 'create customer') in one place.
ProblemSymptomFix
Duplicate rowsSame lead appears twiceFind-or-create with a unique key
Wrong value mappedName in phone fieldRe-test, remap, add a validation filter
Zap stops on blankRun haltedMake the field optional or add a default
Late dataAction runs before the previous record is readyDelay or poll until ready
Key takeaways
  • Use find-or-create and unique IDs.
  • Handle blanks and lists explicitly.
  • Standardise time zones and formats.
Practice: Design the duplicate-protection and missing-data logic for a lead capture Zap.
Advanced · Class 8

AI inside Zapier: classify, summarise, extract and route

Add AI steps safely.

  • Good AI tasks: classify urgency, extract fields from emails and PDFs, summarise threads, draft replies for review, translate, tag feedback.
  • Prompt format: state the task, list allowed labels, request JSON output with fixed keys, and say what to do when unsure ('unknown').
  • Validate: use a Filter or code step to ensure the label is in your list and required fields exist.
  • Human approval: for emails to customers, refunds or edits to records, send a draft to Slack or email for a yes before acting.
  • Privacy: do not send sensitive personal data to AI steps unless your policy and provider terms allow it.
  • Cost and speed: AI steps add time and usage; test with a small batch first.
  • Agents and MCP: Zapier offers AI agent and MCP-style features that let AI assistants use your Zaps as tools; confirm current names and limits in the docs, and restrict which actions an assistant may call.
Prompt example:
Classify this support email. Return JSON only:
{"topic": "refund|delivery|payment|other", "urgency": "low|medium|high", "summary": "max 20 words"}
If unsure use "other" and "low".
Key takeaways
  • Ask for structured JSON and validate it.
  • Keep a human approval step for risky actions.
  • Protect personal data.
Practice: Build the classification prompt and validation rules for support email triage.

Testing, monitoring, versions and team practices

Run automations like a product.

PracticeHow
Test environmentDuplicate the Zap with test sheets or test channels; use test data
Test casesNormal case, blank field, duplicate, long text, special characters, large list
MonitoringEnable error alerts; weekly review of Zap history; track runs and tasks
Version historyDescribe changes; restore if something breaks
RunbookWhat to do if the Zap fails: who, how to replay, how to notify customers

DocumentationDiagram, field map, dependencies (apps, keys, sheets)
Silent failures are the real risk: an automation that stops quietly can cost leads, payments or customer trust. Always alert on errors and check volume against expectations.
Key takeaways
  • Test edge cases, not only the happy path.
  • Alert on errors and watch volumes.
  • Document and review quarterly.
Practice: Write a test plan with 6 cases and a runbook for one Zap.
Advanced · Class 10

Cost control and choosing between Zapier, Make, n8n and code

Pick the right tool for each automation.

ZapierMaken8nCustom code
Ease for beginnersHighestHighMediumLow
App libraryLargestLargeLarge and growing; community nodesAny API
Complex logicGood with paths and code stepsExcellent visual routing and data handlingExcellent, with code and self-hostingUnlimited
Pricing logicPer task (check current)Per operation (check current)Per execution or self-hostEngineering time and hosting
Best forFast business automationsData-heavy multi-step scenariosTechnical teams, privacy, scaleCore product logic

Reduce task usage

  • Add Filters early so non-matching runs stop before using tasks.
  • Combine steps (batch updates) and avoid unnecessary look-ups.
  • Use schedules rather than instant triggers where real-time is not needed.
  • Turn off test Zaps and delete unused ones.
  • Review the top 10 Zaps by usage monthly.

Move to code or n8n when volumes are very high, logic is complex, data is sensitive or you need version control and tests in a repository.

Key takeaways
  • Choose the tool for the job.
  • Filter early to save tasks.
  • Move heavy or sensitive flows to code or self-hosted tools.
Practice: Estimate monthly tasks for your top 3 Zaps and find two ways to cut usage.
Advanced · Class 11

Three complete builds, step by step

Follow detailed blueprints you can reproduce.

Build 1: Lead desk (form to CRM to Slack)

  1. Trigger: Google Forms new response.
  2. Formatter: clean phone and name.
  3. Search CRM contact by email; Path A (found) update; Path B (not found) create.
  4. AI classify budget and urgency into hot / warm / cold.
  5. Filter: hot leads post to Slack with a call-now button; others add to a nurture list.
  6. Delay 2 days; if no reply status, email a follow-up.
  7. Error alert and weekly summary to the owner.

Build 2: Support triage with AI and human approval

  1. Trigger: new ticket or email in the support inbox.
  2. AI step: topic, urgency, language, summary (JSON).
  3. Validation filter: label in allowed list.
  4. Route by topic to the right Slack channel or helpdesk queue.
  5. AI drafts a reply; post draft to Slack with Approve / Edit buttons (interface or Slack message).
  6. On approval send the reply; log in sheet with time to response.

Build 3: Order notifications and stock alerts

  1. Trigger: new order from your store (webhook or app trigger).
  2. Loop through line items; add to inventory sheet.
  3. Send WhatsApp or SMS confirmation with order number and ETA.
  4. If stock below threshold, alert the buyer team with product and quantity.
  5. Daily digest of orders and issues at 6 pm.
Key takeaways
  • Plan trigger, data, branches and alerts before building.
  • Use find-or-create and unique IDs.
  • Add summaries and error alerts.
Practice: Pick one build, create it with test data, and record the test results.

Troubleshooting and FAQ: Zapier

Fix common problems quickly.

ProblemLikely causeFix
Zap did not triggerTrigger is polling (delay), filter blocked it, or the app account is disconnectedCheck Zap history, reconnect, test with a new record, confirm plan polling time
Field is emptySample data lacked the fieldRe-test trigger with live data; map correct field; add default
Duplicate recordsTrigger fires on updateAdd find-or-create and a unique ID
Rate limit errorToo many callsAdd delay, batch or lower frequency
Runs but wrong resultMapping or formatter errorInspect inputs and outputs per step

Debug routine: open the failing run, find the first step with a wrong output, fix that step, retest with the same input, then replay.

  • Use live test data.
  • Filter early to cut usage.

Advanced · Class 13

Practice challenges with solutions: Zapier

Test yourself on realistic tasks.

Challenge 1

Send a Slack alert only when a new lead has budget above Rs 50,000 and is not already in the CRM.

Solution: Trigger → Search CRM by email → Filter (not found AND budget > 50000) → Create contact → Slack message.

Challenge 2

Summarise each day's support emails at 6 pm.

Solution: Schedule 6 pm → Gmail find emails of today → Digest or Looping into a list → AI summary (JSON with topics and counts) → Slack post and Sheet row.

Challenge 3

Create a task for each line item of an order.

Solution: Trigger order → Looping by Zapier on line items → Create task per item with order number and SKU → final Slack message with count.

Challenge 4

Prevent double charges when a payment webhook fires twice.

Solution: Catch Hook → Storage or Tables lookup of the payment ID → Filter (not found) → process → save the payment ID.

Key takeaways
  • Practise filters, searches, loops and digests.
  • Use stored IDs to prevent duplicates.
  • Think through exceptions.
Practice: Create your own three challenges and solutions.

Project, costs, security and limits

Run Zapier reliably and affordably.

Project: lead desk

Website form → AI classification → Hot leads Slack + calendar link; all leads to Sheet; Day-2 follow-up; weekly summary. Add error alerts and an owner.

  • Cost: count tasks per run × expected volume; merge steps; use filters early.
  • Security: least-privilege app connections; don't send personal data you don't need (DPDP); remove old connections.
  • Limits: rate limits and polling delay on free plans; use webhooks for instant triggers.

Interview prep

12 interview questions with answers

What is Zapier?

A no-code tool that connects apps: a trigger in one app runs actions in others.

Trigger vs action?

Trigger starts the Zap when an event happens; actions are the steps that follow.

How do you avoid duplicate records?

Use a Find/Lookup step first, then update or create.

How would you connect a custom website?

Use Webhooks by Zapier's Catch Hook URL and POST JSON from your site.

What is the difference between a Zap and a task?

A Zap is the automation workflow; a task is a counted successful action run, which is typically the billing unit (check current plan rules).

How do you avoid duplicates in Zapier?

Search before creating, store a unique ID, use filters to ignore updates you do not need, and test reruns.

When should you use Paths versus Filters?

Use a Filter to stop a Zap when a condition is not met; use Paths to run different branches for different conditions.

How would you add AI safely in an automation?

Ask for structured output, validate it, send low-confidence or risky cases to a human, protect personal data and monitor results.

How do you debug a failing Zap?

Open the Zap history, inspect the failing step's inputs and outputs, fix the mapping or data, replay, and add tests for that case.

When would you not use Zapier?

For very high volumes, complex logic needing tests and version control, sensitive data that must stay in your systems, or core product features.

How do you control Zapier costs?

Filter early, batch, use schedules when real-time is not needed, remove unused Zaps and monitor top consumers.

How do you secure webhook-triggered Zaps?

Keep the URL secret, validate a shared secret or signature, avoid logging sensitive data and rotate the hook if leaked.

  1. First module: Google Forms/Typeform → Watch Responses (or Webhooks → Custom webhook). Run once to load sample data.
  2. Add Google Sheets → Add a Row; map fields by clicking in a box and picking from the data panel.
  3. Add Gmail → Send an Email; subject "Thanks {{Name}}".
  4. Click Run once, submit a test; see the data bubbles over each module; then switch Scheduling on.
Key takeaways
  • Run once to see data.
  • Map by picking fields.
  • Switch scheduling on.
Practice: Build it and read the execution history for one run.
Basic · Class 3

Make interface tour and your first canvas habits

Get comfortable with the editor and good building habits.

  • Canvas: drag modules, connect with lines, right-click for options; use Run once to test with live data and see bundles at every module.
  • Scenario settings: schedule, sequential processing, data is confidential, max cycles, auto-commit.
  • Mapping panel: click a field to insert data from earlier modules; use functions (formatDate, replace, substring, if, ifempty) for transformations.
  • Naming and notes: rename modules ('Find customer by email') and add notes; future you will be grateful.
  • Folders, teams and organisations: keep scenarios organised and share with teammates.
  • Templates: start from a template, then change the connections and test.
HabitWhy
Test each module as you add itFind mapping errors early
Use filters between modulesStop unwanted bundles and save operations
Build small, then expandEasier to debug
Export a blueprint before big changesSafe backup
Add an error routeNo silent failures
Key takeaways
  • Run once to inspect data at each step.
  • Name modules clearly.
  • Back up with a blueprint.
Practice: Open a template, run it once, and write down what data each module outputs.
Intermediate · Class 4

Flow control: routers, filters, iterators, aggregators

Branch and loop.

ToolUse
RouterSplit into branches, each with a filter (Hot / Warm / Cold)
FilterCondition on the line between modules
IteratorTurn an array (order items) into separate bundles
AggregatorCombine many bundles into one (summary email, one Sheet row)
Set variable / ToolsHold values, sleep, compose text
FunctionsformatDate, ifempty, split, sum…

Iterator and aggregator in a picture

Use Iterator to split an array into items; use an Aggregator (array, text, numeric, table) to join results back into one bundle. Without an aggregator, later modules run once per item.

Key takeaways
  • Router branches, iterator loops, aggregator combines.
  • Filters sit on connections.
  • Use functions for formatting.
Practice: Build a router that sends different emails by lead score.
Intermediate · Class 5

Webhooks, HTTP and JSON

Talk to any API.

  • Custom webhook: gives a URL; click Redetermine data structure after sending a sample.
  • HTTP → Make a request: call any REST API: set method, URL, headers (Authorization: Bearer …), body type JSON; Parse response = yes.
  • JSON module: create or parse JSON; use the data structure builder.
  • AI modules: OpenAI, Claude, Gemini apps or the HTTP module to call any model API.
HTTP request: POST https://api.example.com/v1/leads
Headers: Authorization: Bearer {{key}}   Body (JSON): {"name": "{{Name}}", "email": "{{Email}}"}

JSON basics for automation builders

{
  "order_id": "A-1001",
  "customer": {"name": "Ravi", "phone": "9876543210"},
  "items": [{"sku": "S1", "qty": 2}, {"sku": "S2", "qty": 1}],
  "total": 1499
}
  • Curly braces hold named fields; square brackets hold lists.
  • Use Parse JSON with a data structure so fields appear as mappable items.
  • For HTTP calls: set method, URL, headers (Authorization), query or body, and parse the response.
Key takeaways
  • Webhooks trigger instantly.
  • HTTP module calls any API.
  • Store keys in connections, not text.
Practice: Call a public API with the HTTP module and map two fields.
Intermediate · Class 6

Errors, reliability and templates

Make scenarios dependable.

  • Error handlers: right-click a module → Add error handler: Ignore, Resume (use a default), Rollback, Break (retry later), or Commit.
  • Incomplete executions: turn on to keep failed runs and retry.
  • Notifications: email/Slack alert on errors; name scenarios and use folders.
TemplateFlow
Lead routerWebhook → AI classify → Router → Slack / CRM / nurture
Weekly reportSchedule → Sheet rows → Aggregator → AI summary → email
Order syncShopify order → Iterator items → Sheet rows

Error handling directives

DirectiveWhat it doesUse for
IgnoreSkip the failed bundle and continueNon-critical steps
ResumeSubstitute a default value and continueOptional data
CommitStop and keep what was already donePartial success is acceptable
RollbackStop and undo changes where the apps support itTransactions that must be all-or-nothing
BreakStore as an incomplete execution to retry laterTemporary failures like rate limits
Key takeaways
  • Add error handlers on important modules.
  • Keep incomplete executions.
  • Alert on failures.
Practice: Add a Break handler and an alert to your scenario and force one failure.

Mapping data: functions, dates, text, arrays and JSON

Transform data without code.

TaskFunction / moduleExample

Replace textreplace(text; old; new)Remove spaces from a phone number
Format dateformatDate(date; format; timezone)04 Nov 2026 10:30 in Asia/Kolkata
Add daysaddDays(date; n)Follow-up date
Default valueifempty(value; default)Use 'Unknown' when blank
Conditional textif(condition; a; b)Hot if budget > 50,000 else Warm
Get item from arrayget(array; index) or first()First product name
Sum numberssum(array)Order total
Create JSONCreate JSON / JSON modulePayload to send to another API

Tips: watch data types (text vs number vs date), time zones, and array positions (Make arrays start at 1).

Key takeaways
  • Know your types: text, number, date, array.
  • Use ifempty and if to avoid blanks and errors.
  • Convert time zones deliberately.

Real workflows by role

Copy practical scenarios and adapt them.

RoleScenarioModules in order
Product managerFeedback to backlogWatch rows (Sheet) → HTTP or AI module to classify → Notion/Jira create item → Slack message
MarketingLead capture and nurtureWebhook (form) → Router (hot/cold) → CRM create → email sequence start → data store log

Start with the simplest version, add routers for exceptions and error handlers last.

  • Pick workflows with clear triggers.

Practice: Choose one scenario and draw its module map with error routes.
Intermediate · Class 9

HTTP, APIs, authentication and pagination

Connect to any service, even without a ready-made app.

  • Authentication: API key in a header, bearer token, basic auth, or OAuth 2.0 (use Make's connection support). Store secrets in connections or scenario variables, never in plain notes.
  • Pagination: many APIs return pages; loop with a repeater or 'next page' token until done.
  • Rate limits: add sleep modules or use sequential processing; respect HTTP 429 responses.
  • Webhook security: add a secret in the URL or header and check it in a filter.
  • Idempotency: include unique IDs to prevent duplicate orders or payments if a run is retried.
HTTP statusMeaningAction
200 / 201Success / createdContinue
400Bad requestFix payload
401 / 403Not allowedCheck key or scope
404Not foundCheck ID or URL
429Too many requestsWait and retry
500+Server errorRetry later; alert if repeated
Key takeaways
  • Use connections for secrets.
  • Handle pagination and rate limits.
  • Include unique IDs to avoid duplicates.
Practice: Call a public API (for example a weather or currency API) from Make and save results to a sheet.
Advanced · Class 10

Reliability: error routes, retries, data stores and locking

Make scenarios resilient.

ProblemDesign
Temporary outageBreak directive with automatic retries; alert if retries exhausted
Bad data in one bundleError route that logs the bundle to a sheet and notifies the owner; continue others
Duplicate runsStore processed IDs in a data store and skip if seen
Order of processing mattersEnable sequential processing; use queues
Two scenarios editing the same recordUse a lock flag in a data store or process via one scenario
Large volumesProcess in batches; schedule off-peak; split scenarios
MonitoringEmail or Slack alerts on error, daily summary of runs and failures

Incomplete executions

When Break is used, failed runs wait in Incomplete executions. Review daily, fix the cause, and run them again.

Key takeaways
  • Create an error route for every important scenario.
  • Use data stores to remember what is done.
  • Review incomplete executions regularly.
Practice: Add error handling and duplicate protection to a scenario that creates CRM contacts.
Advanced · Class 11

AI in Make, agents and responsible use

Add AI steps with control.

  • AI modules: classify, extract, summarise, translate and draft using providers such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Gemini through ready modules or HTTP calls; Make also offers its own AI features and agent-style tools (confirm current names in the docs).
  • Pattern: collect input → AI with structured JSON output → parse → validate (router with filters) → act or send to human → log.
  • Cost: each AI call adds provider tokens and one or more operations; monitor both.
  • Safety: avoid sending sensitive data unless allowed; ask AI to return 'unknown' when unsure; require human approval for customer-facing or money-related actions.
  • Prompt versions: keep prompts in a data store or note with a version and test cases.
Use casePrompt outputValidation
Lead scoring{score: 1-10, reason}Score is a number 1-10
Invoice extraction{vendor, date, amount, tax}Amount > 0, date valid, totals match
Feedback tagging{topic, sentiment}Topic in allowed list
Key takeaways
  • Ask for JSON and validate it.
  • Monitor provider cost and operations.
  • Human approval for risky actions.
Practice: Design the router and validation logic for an AI invoice-extraction scenario.
Advanced · Class 12

Cost control, governance and choosing Make vs Zapier vs n8n

Run automations at scale and pick the right tool.

LeverHow it reduces operations
Filter earlyStop unwanted bundles before costly modules
AggregateSend one message or API call instead of many
Use schedulesPoll less often when real-time is not needed
Webhooks over pollingInstant and cheaper than frequent polling
Avoid unnecessary searchesPass IDs instead of searching again
Clean upTurn off test scenarios; review top consumers monthly

Governance

  • Use an organisation account with roles; avoid personal connections.
  • Keep an inventory: purpose, owner, data used, apps, last review.
  • Peer review changes to critical scenarios; export blueprints as backups.
  • Define who gets alerts and who fixes.
ChooseWhen
MakeVisual, data-heavy workflows with routers, iterators and detailed control
ZapierFast simple automations and the widest app coverage
n8nTechnical teams, self-hosting, privacy, custom code and scale
CodeCore product logic and heavy workloads
Key takeaways
  • Filter, aggregate and schedule wisely.
  • Inventory and review automations.
  • Pick the tool by logic complexity and data sensitivity.
Practice: Estimate operations for your top scenarios and choose two cost-saving changes.
Advanced · Class 13

Three complete scenarios, step by step

Reproduce detailed builds.

Scenario 1: Webhook lead intake with scoring

  1. Custom webhook receives form data.
  2. Set variables: clean phone, name, normalised email.
  3. Search CRM by email; router: update or create.
  4. AI module scores 1 to 10 with reason (JSON); parse JSON.
  5. Router: score ≥ 8 → Slack alert + task for sales; else → add to nurture sequence.
  6. Data store: save lead ID to prevent duplicates; error route emails the owner.

Scenario 2: Order with many items to inventory and confirmation

  1. Webhook receives order JSON; parse JSON.
  2. Iterator over items; for each, update stock in sheet or database.
  3. Aggregator builds a summary text; send confirmation by email or WhatsApp.
  4. Router: if any item below threshold → alert the purchasing channel.
  5. Error handler: commit what succeeded and log failures to a sheet.

Scenario 3: Daily operations digest

  1. Scheduler at 8:00 on weekdays.
  2. HTTP modules fetch orders, tickets and failures (with pagination).
  3. Aggregate counts and top issues; AI writes a 5-line summary.
  4. Build an HTML email with a table; send to the leadership list; archive in Drive.
Key takeaways
  • Parse, validate, route, act, log.
  • Protect against duplicates and failures.
  • Summaries help humans stay in control.
Practice: Build one scenario with test data and run it 10 times, including a failure case.

ProblemLikely causeFix

Advanced · Class 15

Practice challenges with solutions: Make

Test yourself on realistic tasks.

Challenge 1

Receive orders by webhook and email a single summary per order, even with many items.

Solution: Webhook → Parse JSON → Iterator (items) → Text aggregator (lines) → Email with the combined text.

Challenge 2

Fetch 500 records from a paginated API into a sheet.

Solution: Repeater or loop with page token → HTTP GET → Parse JSON → Iterator → Sheet add row; stop when next token is empty.

Challenge 3

Skip records already processed.

Solution: Data store: search by ID → Filter (not found) → process → add ID to the store.

Challenge 4

Alert if any run fails.

Solution: Add an error handler route with Break plus a Slack module with scenario name, bundle info and a link to the execution.

Key takeaways
  • Combine iterator, aggregator, store and error routes.
  • Think about pagination and retries.
  • Always add alerts.
Practice: Create your own three challenges with solutions.
Advanced · Class 16

Project and cost control

Ship a scenario you can show.

Project: AI lead router

Website form (webhook) → AI classifies and summarises → Router: Hot → Slack + calendar link; Warm → nurture email; Cold → Sheet. Weekly aggregator report. Error handlers + alerts.

  • Cost: operations = modules × runs; filter early, avoid polling when a webhook exists, combine steps.
  • Security: private connections, minimal personal data, rotate API keys.
Key takeaways
  • Filter early to save operations.
  • Prefer webhooks to polling.
  • Document owner and alerts.

Interview prep

12 interview questions with answers

What is Make?

A visual no-code automation builder with modules connected into scenarios.

Iterator vs aggregator?

Iterator splits an array into bundles; aggregator merges bundles into one.

How do you handle errors?

Add error handlers (ignore, resume, rollback, break), keep incomplete executions, and alert.

When choose Make over Zapier?

For branching, loops, API calls and cost-efficiency; Zapier for the widest app library and simplicity.

What is the difference between an operation and a bundle in Make?

A bundle is one item of data; an operation is one module processing one bundle. Operations are typically what counts toward the plan (check current rules).

When do you use an iterator and an aggregator?

Use an iterator to split an array into individual items and an aggregator to combine results back into a single bundle.

How do you handle errors in Make?

Add error routes with directives: ignore, resume, commit, rollback or break, and review incomplete executions; alert owners.

How do you prevent duplicate processing?

Store processed IDs in a data store, search before creating, and use idempotency keys when calling APIs.

How would you connect an app with no module?

Use the HTTP module with the API's authentication, parse the JSON response, and handle pagination and rate limits.

How do you secure webhooks?

Use a secret in the URL or header, validate it, restrict logging of sensitive data, and rotate if exposed.

How do you reduce operations usage?

Filter early, aggregate, use webhooks instead of polling, schedule wisely and remove unused scenarios.

Make or Zapier?

Make for visual, data-heavy, multi-branch scenarios; Zapier for fast simple automations and the largest app library; choose after testing a real workflow in each.

Basic · Class 2

Build your first app with Agent

From prompt to running app.

  1. Prompt with a mini-PRD: "Build a web app 'Class Booking' for a yoga studio: home, class list, book a slot (name, phone), my bookings. Calm green style. Save bookings in a database."
  2. Review the Agent's plan; approve; watch files being created.
  3. Use Preview; click through; note bugs.
  4. Fix by chat: "The booking form doesn't clear after saving. Fix and add a success message." One change at a time.
  5. Use the checkpoints/history to roll back if something breaks.

A mini-PRD prompt that works

Build a leave-request web app for a 30-person company.
Users: Employee (submit, see status), Manager (approve or reject), HR (see all, export CSV).
Pages: Login, My requests, New request, Team requests (manager), Admin (HR).
Data: users(name, email, role), requests(user, type, start, end, reason, status).
Rules: end date after start; managers see only their team; email on decision.
Style: clean, mobile-friendly, blue accent.
Start with the data model and the employee flow only. Ask me before adding anything else.

Ask the Agent to plan first, review the plan, then let it build in small steps, checking the preview after each step.

Key takeaways
  • Start with a mini-PRD.
  • One change per prompt.
  • Roll back with history.
Practice: Build the booking app and fix 3 issues by chat.

Intermediate · Class 6

Prompting the Agent like a product manager

Write specs, checkpoints and reviews that get reliable results.

  • Describe outcomes and rules, not code: users, pages, data, rules, edge cases, visuals.
  • Slice the work: authentication, then data model, then main flow, then polish. Large vague prompts create tangled apps.
  • Give examples: sample records, example emails, screenshots.
  • Say what must not change: 'Do not change the login page'.
  • Debugging prompt: 'When I click Submit on the New Request page, nothing happens. The console shows [error]. Find the cause, explain it, then fix it.'
  • Use checkpoints: restore if the Agent breaks something; commit working versions to Git.
  • Ask for explanations: 'Summarise what you changed and any risks.'
Weak promptStrong prompt
Make a nice dashboardCreate a dashboard with 3 cards (open requests, approved this month, average response time) and a table of requests with filters by status and date
Fix the bugDescribe steps, expected vs actual result, error text, and what changed just before
Add paymentsAdd a Razorpay hosted checkout for the Pro plan at Rs 799, store the payment ID, and mark the user as Pro only after the webhook confirms
Key takeaways
  • Slice the work and review each slice.
  • Write rules and edge cases in the prompt.
  • Use checkpoints and Git for safety.
Practice: Write a mini-PRD prompt and a debugging prompt for an app idea of your own.
Intermediate · Class 7

Three practical builds: internal tool, landing page with leads, and an API or bot

Build examples PMs actually need.

Build 1: Internal request tracker

  1. Prompt the data model (requests, users, roles).
  2. Add login and roles (employee, manager).
  3. Build the form, list and approval flow.
  4. Add email or Slack notification via a secret key.
  5. Test with two accounts; deploy as Autoscale.

Build 2: Landing page with waitlist

  1. Create a one-page site with hero, features, FAQ and sign-up form.
  2. Store sign-ups in the database; prevent duplicates by email.
  3. Send a confirmation email; add a privacy notice and consent checkbox.
  4. Add analytics events (page view, sign-up).
  5. Deploy as Static or Autoscale; connect a custom domain.

Build 3: Small API or bot

  1. Define endpoints (for example GET /status, POST /order).
  2. Add authentication via an API key in Secrets.
  3. Log requests; add rate limiting.
  4. Deploy on a reserved VM if it must stay always on (for example a Telegram or WhatsApp-style bot using the provider's API).

Intermediate · Class 8

Data, authentication and integrations in detail

Design the data and logins properly.

TopicGuidance
Data modelList entities (users, orders), fields and relationships; ask the Agent to create tables and migrations; avoid changing structures casually once real data exists
AuthenticationUse a built-in or well-known auth service; support password reset; consider login with Google; never build your own crypto
AuthorisationCheck roles and ownership on the server for every request
Environment separationUse separate databases or keys for testing and production
IntegrationsUse official SDKs and API keys in Secrets; handle errors and rate limits; verify webhooks (signatures)
Email and notificationsUse a transactional email provider; test with a sandbox
PaymentsUse hosted checkout and webhooks; do not trust the browser alone to say a payment succeeded
FilesLimit types and sizes; scan or restrict public access
Migration tip: before changing a database structure with real data, ask the Agent to write a migration, test it on a copy, and keep a backup.
Key takeaways
  • Model data first; protect it with auth and roles.
  • Separate test and production.
  • Confirm payments server-side.
Practice: Draw the data model and roles for an app idea, then prompt the Agent to implement only that.
Advanced · Class 9

Quality, security and performance checklist

Make your app safe enough to share.

CheckWhyHow
Secrets never in code or chatKeys in prompts or repos leak and get abusedUse the Secrets panel or environment variables; rotate any key you pasted by mistake
Authentication and rolesAnyone with the link could see private dataRequire login for private pages; check roles on the server, not only in the UI
Input validationBad input causes errors and attacksValidate types and lengths; escape output; use parameterised queries
Row-level or per-user data rulesUsers must only see their own dataDefine rules in the database; test with two accounts
Rate limits and abuse controlBots can run up costsLimit sign-ups, form posts and AI calls; add CAPTCHA if needed
Payment handlingCard data is regulatedUse a hosted checkout (for example Razorpay, Stripe); never store card numbers
Privacy and consentPersonal data laws apply (DPDP Act)Collect minimum data, show a privacy notice, allow deletion
Backups and recoveryMistakes and bad deploys happenUse checkpoints, version control and database backups; test a restore

Quality and performance

  • Testing: ask the Agent to write tests for key flows; run them before deploying; test on a phone.
  • Error handling: friendly messages, logs, alerts for failures.
  • Performance: avoid loading everything at once; paginate lists; compress images; check load time on 4G.
  • Accessibility: labels, contrast, keyboard use.
  • Observability: view logs and add basic analytics and uptime checks.
Key takeaways
  • Security basics are mandatory before sharing.
  • Test with two users and on a phone.
  • Log errors and watch costs.
Practice: Run the checklist on one of your apps and fix the top five findings.
Advanced · Class 10

Git, collaboration, environments and handing over to engineers

Work with developers and move beyond a prototype.

  • Git and GitHub: commit often; use branches for risky changes; connect to a GitHub repository so engineers can review and extend.
  • Collaboration: invite teammates; agree who prompts the Agent to avoid conflicting changes.
  • Environments: development, staging, production with separate keys and data.
  • Handoff package: repository link, README (purpose, how to run), environment variable list (names only), data model diagram, known issues, security review notes and next steps.
  • When to hand off: real customers, payments, personal data, scale, compliance needs or complex integrations.
StageOwnerOutput
Idea and prototypePM using AgentWorking prototype and learnings
HardeningEngineerTests, security, performance, monitoring
ProductionEngineering teamScalable, supported system
Key takeaways
  • Use Git from day one.
  • Prepare a handoff package.
  • Know when to graduate to engineering.
Practice: Write the README and handoff list for a Replit app you built.

Interview prep

12 interview questions with answers

What is Replit Agent?

An AI that builds, runs and fixes apps in Replit from plain-English descriptions.

Where do API keys go?

In Secrets (environment variables), never in code or chat.

How do you deploy?

Use Deploy, pick a deployment type, add secrets, and optionally a custom domain.

Replit vs Lovable?

Replit gives a full coding environment with many languages and backends; Lovable focuses on front-end web apps with Supabase and GitHub sync.

What is Replit Agent best used for?

Turning a clear description into a working app quickly: prototypes, internal tools and small services, with a human reviewing and testing.

How do you write a good prompt for an AI app builder?

Describe users, pages, data, rules and edge cases, work in small slices, give examples, say what must not change, and ask for a plan before building.

How do you keep secrets safe?

Store them in Secrets or environment variables, never in code, prompts or repositories, and rotate any key that was exposed.

What are the deployment options and when to use them?

Static for simple sites, Autoscale for apps with variable traffic, Reserved VM for always-on services, and Scheduled for timed jobs (confirm current options).

What security checks matter before sharing an AI-built app?

Secrets, authentication and roles, validation, per-user data rules, rate limits, safe payments, privacy and backups.

When should you hand an AI-built app to engineers?

When it has real customers, payments, personal data, scale or compliance needs, or when logic and integrations become complex.

How do you control costs when building with an Agent?

Keep prompts focused, work in slices, stop loops, watch usage and budgets, and avoid unnecessary rebuilds.

How do you debug with an Agent?

Give steps, expected and actual results and error messages, ask for the cause and an explanation before the fix, and test again.

Basic · Class 2

Write prompts that build well

Use a mini-PRD for the first prompt.

App: Class Booking for a yoga studio in Pune.
Users: members and studio admin.
Pages: Home, Classes (list + filter), Class detail with Book button, My bookings, Admin (add/edit classes, see bookings).
Style: calm, green and cream, rounded cards, mobile-first.
Data: classes (title, trainer, date/time, seats), bookings (member, class).
Rules: a class can't be booked when full; confirmation message after booking.
  • Name pages, data, rules and style; ask for sample data.
  • Then iterate one change at a time: "Add a pricing page with 3 plans."
  • Paste screenshots or reference sites for visual direction.

Prompt formula: ROLE, GOAL, SCREENS, DATA, RULES, STYLE

You are building a clinic appointment app.
Goal: patients book a 15-minute slot with a doctor and get a confirmation.
Screens: Home, Doctor list, Doctor detail with calendar, Booking form, My bookings, Admin (doctors, slots).
Data: doctors(name, speciality, fee), slots(doctor, start, status), bookings(patient, slot, status).
Rules: no double booking; patients see only their bookings; admins manage slots.
Style: calm green, large text, mobile first, English and Hindi labels.
  • Start with layout and mock data, then connect real data.
  • One feature per prompt; test; then move on.
  • Use screenshots or sketches for layout and say 'keep everything else unchanged'.
Key takeaways
  • Mini-PRD first prompt.
  • One change at a time.
  • Screenshots help.
Practice: Write a mini-PRD prompt and build the first version.
Intermediate · Class 3

Data and login with Supabase

Add a database and user accounts.

  1. Connect Supabase (button in the project); create or link a project.
  2. Ask: "Create tables for classes and bookings with row-level security; members see only their own bookings; admins see all."
  3. Ask for sign-up/login (email and Google) and an admin role.
  4. Test as a member and as an admin; check that one user can't see another's data.
  5. Keep secret keys in the backend/edge-function secrets, never in the front end.

Supabase concepts in plain words

ConceptMeaning
TablesWhere records live (like spreadsheets)
AuthenticationSign-up, login, password reset, social login
Row Level Security (RLS)Rules that decide which rows each user may read or change
PoliciesThe actual RLS rules, for example 'a user can see rows where user_id equals their ID'
StorageBuckets for files and images
Edge FunctionsSmall server-side code for secrets, payments and third-party calls
SecretsKeys stored on the server side, never in the front-end
Never put secret keys in front-end code. Use edge functions for payment secrets and private API keys; the public (anon) key is designed to be exposed but is only safe when RLS is correct.
Key takeaways
  • Supabase = database + auth.
  • Row-level security protects data.
  • Test with two users.
Practice: Add login and two tables; prove users can't see each other's bookings.
Intermediate · Class 4

GitHub sync and publishing

Own your code and go live.

  1. GitHub: connect, create a repo; changes sync both ways, so a developer (or Claude Code/Codex) can continue the project.
  2. Publish: click Publish for a public URL.
  3. Custom domain: project settings → Domains → add your domain; copy the DNS records to your registrar; wait for HTTPS.
  4. After launch: add analytics (GA4/Clarity), SEO titles and a privacy page.

Publishing checklist

  • Test sign-up, login, logout, password reset and the main flow with two accounts.
  • Check mobile layout and speed.
  • Set page titles, descriptions and share images.
  • Connect a custom domain with HTTPS.
  • Add privacy policy and terms pages; add cookie notice if needed.
Key takeaways
  • Sync to GitHub for ownership.
  • Domains need DNS records.
  • Add analytics and privacy page.
Practice: Publish your app on a custom domain or subdomain.

NeedPrompt
Landing page"Add a hero, 3 benefits, testimonials, pricing and FAQ; make the CTA 'Book a free call'."
Contact form"Add a form (name, phone, message) that saves to Supabase and emails me."
Dashboard"Add an admin dashboard with bookings per week and a table with filters."
