Interview prep

14 interview questions with answers

Why is AI pricing different?

Each use has variable model cost, so heavy usage can destroy margins on flat seat pricing.

Which pricing model would you choose?

The one whose metric matches customer value and cost: often hybrid seat + included usage + overage, or outcome pricing when results are measurable.

How do you calculate cost per task?

Tokens × prices × calls + tools and retrieval + human review share, divided over successful tasks.

How do you protect margins?

Routing, caching, context trimming, step caps, batching, monitoring cost per task, verified with evals.

How do you sell AI?

Outcome proof, fast time-to-value, trust answers, ROI tools.

How do you price an AI product?

Start from customer value, model the cost per use, choose a value metric (seat, usage, outcome or credits), package good-better-best tiers with caps, and validate with research and pilots.

Seat-based or usage-based pricing for AI?

Seats are simple but break when AI does work without users. Usage aligns with cost but can scare buyers; hybrids with included credits and overage are common.

How do you protect margins in an AI product?

Model routing, caching, prompt optimisation, caps and fair use, batch discounts, annual commits, and regular re-pricing based on real cost data.

What is the heavy-user problem?

A few users consume far more cost than they pay for, harming gross margin. Solve with limits, usage tiers or credits.

How do you design a free tier?

Limit cost per free user, show value fast, upgrade at limits or premium features, and prevent abuse with verification and rate limits.

What is outcome-based pricing?

Charging per result, such as a resolved ticket. It aligns incentives but requires clear measurement and volume protection.

How do you raise prices without losing customers?

Communicate value, give notice, grandfather where sensible, pilot with new customers, and monitor churn and support.

What do enterprise buyers ask about AI vendors?

Security certifications, data use and residency, SLAs, IP indemnity, quality guarantees, pricing structure and ROI evidence.

Model prices are falling. What does it mean for pricing?

Costs drop for everyone, so differentiation must come from value, workflow and trust; decide whether to cut price, add features or increase margin.

Problem typeQuestion it answersProduct exampleTypical output
ClassificationWhich category?Is this transaction fraud? Is this review spam?Label and probability
RegressionHow much?Delivery time, price estimate, demandA number
Ranking / recommendationWhat first?Search results, home feed, 'frequently bought together'Ordered list
ClusteringWhat groups exist?Customer segments, similar storesGroup IDs
Anomaly detectionWhat is unusual?Payment spike, server faultScore and alert
ForecastingWhat happens next?Sales next week, rider demand by hourTime series
NLP / generativeWhat does this say, or write thisSupport triage, summaries, chatText
Computer visionWhat is in this image?Document OCR, product photo qualityLabels, boxes, text
Before using ML, ask: Could a rule or a simple lookup do 80% of the job? ML shines where rules are too many, change often, or depend on patterns humans cannot write down.
Key takeaways
  • Name the problem type first.
  • Each type has different metrics.
  • Many products combine types.
Practice: Name the ML problem type for 8 features in apps you use.
Basic · Class 2

Data and labelling

Get the data an ML product needs.

  • Labels from outcomes (did the user default?), humans (annotators), or rules.
  • Watch leakage (using future information), class imbalance (rare fraud), and bias.
  • Labelling tools and vendors; clear guidelines and agreement checks.

Data quality checklist

CheckQuestion
CoverageDo we have data for all user types, regions, devices and seasons?
Label qualityDo two annotators agree? What is the agreement rate?
FreshnessHow old is it? Does behaviour change quickly?
LeakageDoes a feature contain information from the future or the answer itself?
ImbalanceIs the thing we want to predict rare (fraud 0.1%)?
BiasDoes the data under-represent groups?
Consent and privacyDo we have the right to use it for this purpose?

Labelling approaches: use existing outcomes (a returned order = label), human annotators with guidelines, domain experts for hard cases, weak labels from rules, and active learning (label the examples the model is unsure about). Always keep a clean golden set for evaluation.

Key takeaways
  • Data quality decides model quality.
  • Write labelling guidelines.
  • Check leakage, imbalance and bias.
Practice: Write labelling guidelines for classifying support tickets into 6 categories.
Intermediate · Class 3

Metrics and trade-offs

Choose model metrics that match business costs.

  • Precision = of flagged, how many were right; recall = of all positives, how many we caught.
  • Choose thresholds by business cost: missing fraud vs annoying good customers.
  • Link model metrics to product metrics (approval rate, losses, CSAT) with A/B tests.

Worked example: fraud detection with a cost matrix

Out of 100,000 payments, 200 are fraud. Model A flags 1,000 payments and catches 160 frauds (precision 16%, recall 80%). Model B flags 300 and catches 120 frauds (precision 40%, recall 60%).

Model AModel B
Frauds caught160120
Frauds missed (cost Rs 3,000 each)40 x 3,000 = Rs 1,20,00080 x 3,000 = Rs 2,40,000
Good users flagged (cost Rs 100 each in review and friction)840 x 100 = Rs 84,000180 x 100 = Rs 18,000
Total costRs 2,04,000Rs 2,58,000

Model A costs less overall, even though Model B has higher precision. Choose the threshold from business cost, not from a default of 0.5. Also watch the experience of the 840 good users flagged by A; add step-up verification instead of a hard block.

MetricMeaningWhen it matters
PrecisionOf those flagged, how many were rightCost of false alarms is high
RecallOf all true cases, how many were foundCost of misses is high
F1Balance of the twoSingle-number comparisons
AUC (ROC)Ranking quality across thresholdsComparing models
MAE / RMSEAverage error size (regression)ETA, price, demand
NDCG, MRR, hit-rateQuality of ranked listsSearch and recommendations
Key takeaways
  • Precision vs recall is a business decision.
  • Set thresholds by cost of errors.
  • Validate with online experiments.
Practice: For a loan-default model, decide which error is worse and how you'd set the threshold.
Intermediate · Class 4

Recommendations and personalisation

Understand how recommenders work and are measured.

  • Approaches: popularity, collaborative filtering (people like you), content-based (similar items), and hybrid/deep models.
  • Cold start for new users/items: onboarding questions, popular items, content features.
  • Metrics: CTR, conversion, watch time, diversity, novelty, long-term retention.
  • Guardrails: filter bubbles, fairness to sellers/creators, safety.

Recommendation approaches

ApproachHow it worksStrengthWeakness
PopularityShow what most people likeSimple, strong baselineNot personal
Content-basedRecommend items similar to what you liked (using item features or embeddings)Works for new itemsNarrow, repetitive
Collaborative filteringPeople like you liked theseFinds surprising matchesCold start for new users and items
Hybrid / deep modelsCombine signals with learned embeddingsBest accuracyComplexity, cost, explainability
BanditsExplore new options while exploiting known good onesLearns fastNeeds careful design
  • Cold start: use popularity, onboarding questions and item metadata until behaviour data exists.
  • Beyond accuracy: diversity, novelty, fairness to sellers, freshness, and business rules (stock, margin).
  • Feedback loops: showing only popular items makes them more popular; reserve slots for exploration.
Key takeaways
  • Hybrid recommenders are common.
  • Plan for cold start.
  • Balance engagement with diversity and long-term value.
Practice: Design recommendations for a regional-language news app.
Intermediate · Class 5

ML use cases by industry and how they work

See what ML does in e-commerce, fintech and services, with data and metrics.

IndustryUse caseHow it worksData neededMetric
E-commerceSearch rankingRank products by relevance, price, stock and past clicks using a learning-to-rank modelQueries, clicks, add-to-cart, purchasesSearch conversion, NDCG, zero-result rate
E-commerceRecommendationsSuggest next products from behaviour and item embeddingsViews, orders, catalogueCTR, add-to-cart, revenue per session
Quick commerceETA and demand predictionRegression on distance, store load, rider supply, weatherPast orders and ridesETA error, on-time rate, cost per order
FintechCredit scoringClassification of default risk using bureau and behavioural dataApplications, repayment historyApproval rate, default rate, fairness gaps
FintechFraud detectionReal-time scoring of transactions with rules plus modelsTransactions, device, locationFraud loss, false-positive rate, latency
InsuranceClaims triageClassify claims and estimate severity; route to the right teamPast claims, documentsCycle time, leakage
HealthcareTriage and imaging supportClassify symptoms or images to prioritise casesLabelled records and imagesSensitivity, specificity, clinician time saved
MarketingChurn and next-best-actionPredict who will leave; choose the offerUsage, billing, support historyRetention uplift, cost per saved customer

Pattern: prediction alone creates no value. Connect each prediction to a decision and an action (block, review, offer, reroute), and measure the action's outcome.

Key takeaways
  • A prediction needs a decision and an action to create value.
  • Pick metrics that reflect the business outcome.
  • Know the data each use case needs before committing.
Practice: For one industry, write the prediction, the action it triggers, the data needed and the metric.
Intermediate · Class 6

Offline vs online evaluation and experimentation

Test models safely before and after launch.

  • Offline evaluation (precision, AUC, NDCG) is fast and cheap but can mislead: history is not the future, and the model changes user behaviour.
  • Shadow mode: the model scores real traffic silently so you compare it to the current system without affecting users.
  • Online A/B test: randomise users; primary metric tied to the business (conversion, fraud loss), guardrails (latency, complaints, fairness), enough sample and time to cover weekly cycles.
  • Interleaving (for ranking) mixes results from two rankers in one list to detect preference with less traffic.
  • Counterfactual and bandit methods help when random tests are costly.
  • Novelty effects: early excitement can fade; run long enough.
Pitfall: a model with a better offline score can lose online because of latency, odd edge cases, or feedback loops. Always confirm online.
Key takeaways
  • Offline metrics are necessary, not sufficient.
  • Use shadow, canary and A/B stages.
  • Pick guardrails as carefully as the primary metric.
Practice: Design a staged evaluation plan for a new search ranking model.
Advanced · Class 7

Model lifecycle and MLOps

Keep models working after launch.

  • Shadow mode and gradual rollout before full launch.
  • Monitor data drift, prediction drift and business metrics; alert on drops.
  • Model registry and versioning; rollback plans.
  • Model cards documenting purpose, data, limits.

MLOps is the practice of running that loop reliably: version data, code and models; automate training and testing; deploy safely (shadow, canary); monitor quality and cost; retrain on triggers.

Key takeaways
  • Launch is the start of the lifecycle.
  • Monitor drift and business impact.
  • Always have a rollback.
Practice: Write a monitoring plan for a delivery-ETA model.
Advanced · Class 8

Deployment, monitoring and drift

Keep ML models healthy in production.

TopicWhat PMs should know
Batch vs real-timeBatch scores many items on a schedule (cheap, stale). Real-time scores on request (fresh, needs low latency and robust infrastructure).
Latency budgetTotal time allowed (for example 100 ms for a payment decision), split across feature lookup, model and rules.
Feature storeA shared place for computed features so training and serving use identical logic (avoids training-serving skew).
Model registry and versioningEvery model has a version, data lineage, metrics, owner, and rollback path.
Data driftInputs change (new device types, new city). Detect with distribution checks.
Concept driftThe relationship changes (new fraud tactics). Detect with quality metrics against fresh labels.
Retraining triggersSchedule, drift alert, performance drop, major product change.
FallbacksRules, previous model or a safe default when the model fails or is slow.
CostCompute for training and serving, storage, labelling; track cost per prediction.

Monitoring dashboard: data quality, input drift, prediction distribution, business KPIs, latency, errors, cost, fairness slices, and alerts with owners.

Key takeaways
  • Plan monitoring and fallbacks before launch.
  • Drift is normal; build retraining into the roadmap.
  • Track cost and latency, not only accuracy.
Practice: Design a monitoring and fallback plan for a real-time fraud model.
Advanced · Class 9

Writing an ML product requirements document

Specify ML features so data scientists and engineers can build the right thing.

SectionWhat to write
Problem and usersWho benefits, what decision changes, current process and baseline
Success metricsBusiness metric, model metric, guardrails, targets and the acceptable range
DataSources, volume, labels, freshness, consent, known gaps
Model requirementsLatency, throughput, explainability, fairness, privacy, offline vs real-time
Thresholds and actionsWhat happens at each score band (approve, review, block)
Fallback and human reviewWhat happens when the model is unsure or down
Evaluation planOffline set, shadow, A/B, timeline
RisksBias, drift, abuse, regulation, dependence on a vendor
MilestonesData readiness, baseline, prototype, pilot, rollout, with uncertainty acknowledged
Estimating ML work: data work often takes longer than modelling. Plan an early baseline (rules or a simple model) to learn what is possible, then set targets with ranges, not promises.
Key takeaways
  • Specify decisions, thresholds and fallbacks, not just 'build a model'.
  • Start with a baseline.
  • Express timelines as ranges.
Practice: Write an ML PRD outline for a churn-prediction feature.
Advanced · Class 10

Case studies: fraud detection and recommendations end to end

Walk two complete ML products from problem to monitoring.

Case 1: real-time payment fraud (fintech)

  1. Problem: fraud losses are 0.12% of volume; manual review is slow.
  2. Baseline: rules (new device + high amount) catch 45% of fraud with many false alarms.
  3. Model: gradient-boosted trees on device, velocity, location, payee and history; score under 50 ms.
  4. Actions: low risk approve; medium step-up (OTP or biometric); high block and review.
  5. Evaluation: offline on past fraud; shadow for 2 weeks; A/B on 10%.
  6. Guardrails: payment success rate, step-up completion, complaints from blocked genuine users.
  7. Monitoring: daily drift, weekly new-pattern review, retrain monthly.

Case 2: home-feed recommendations (e-commerce)

  1. Problem: low repeat rate; users scroll but do not find items.
  2. Baseline: popular items by category.
  3. Model: two-stage: candidate generation (embeddings from views and orders) then ranking (clicks and purchase probability with price, stock, margin).
  4. Cold start: onboarding choices and trending items for new users.
  5. Metrics: add-to-cart per session, orders per user, diversity, seller exposure; guardrail: page speed.
  6. Risks: popularity bias, filter bubbles, stale stock; fix with exploration slots and real-time inventory checks.
Key takeaways
  • Start with a rules or popularity baseline.
  • Connect scores to actions with thresholds.
  • Plan guardrails and monitoring from day one.
Practice: Choose one case and write the full plan using the seven steps.
Advanced · Class 11

Case studies: ETA prediction and churn prediction

Work through two ML products end to end (illustrative).

Case 1: ETA prediction for 10-minute delivery

  1. Problem: customers cancel when ETAs are wrong; the rule-based ETA is off by 4 minutes on average.
  2. Data: distance, store load, picker queue, rider supply, traffic, weather, time of day.
  3. Model: regression (gradient boosting) predicting delivery time and a prediction interval.
  4. Metric: mean absolute error (MAE) and share of orders within 2 minutes of the promised ETA; business: cancellation rate and NPS.
  5. Action: show ETA ranges, adjust dispatch when late risk is high.
  6. Risks: underestimates hurt trust more than overestimates; add a safety buffer by percentile (p80).
  7. Monitoring: weekly error by city and hour; drift alert on rainy days.

Case 2: Churn prediction for a subscription app

  1. Problem: 8% monthly churn; retention offers are expensive.
  2. Target: will cancel in the next 30 days.
  3. Evaluation: precision at top 10% (who to contact), uplift (did the offer change behaviour?).
  4. Action: send tailored offers only to users who are likely to churn and likely to respond; leave others alone.
  5. Experiment: randomise a hold-out group to measure true saves.
  6. Risk: offering discounts to people who would have stayed.
Key takeaways
  • Match metric to the decision.
  • Use uplift thinking when actions cost money.
  • Monitor by segment and condition.
Practice: Write a plan for another prediction product (stock-out prediction) using the same steps.
Advanced · Class 12

Interview practice: ML product scenario questions

Practise ML product thinking without code.

Q. How would you build a fraud detection product?
Model answer: I would define loss and friction costs, start with rules as a baseline, collect labelled fraud outcomes, build a model scoring in real time, set thresholds from a cost matrix with step-up verification for medium risk, run shadow mode then A/B, and monitor drift, false positives and complaints. I would work with data science on features and with risk on policy.
Why it works: It covers baseline, labels, thresholds, rollout and monitoring.
Q. The model's accuracy is 99% but the business is not happy. Why?
Model answer: Accuracy can hide class imbalance: if fraud is 1% of cases, predicting 'no fraud' gives 99%. I would use precision, recall, cost-based metrics and business outcomes by segment.
Why it works: Shows understanding of imbalance.
Q. How do you decide when to retrain a model?
Model answer: Triggers: scheduled cadence, data or concept drift, performance drop on fresh labels, or product changes. I would define monitoring thresholds, an automated pipeline and a rollback plan.
Why it works: Operational thinking.
Q. How do you explain a model decision to a customer?
Model answer: Use reason codes tied to understandable factors, avoid revealing sensitive internals that enable gaming, provide an appeal path, and keep logs for audits.
Why it works: Balances transparency and safety.
Key takeaways
  • Use cost-based thinking.
  • Know accuracy pitfalls.
  • Plan retraining and monitoring.
Practice: Answer the fraud question using a cost matrix with your own numbers.
Advanced · Class 13

Working with data scientists and final project

Collaborate well and ship an ML feature.

  • PM brings: problem, users, business costs of errors, constraints, success metric.
  • DS brings: feasibility, data needs, model choice, offline metrics.
  • Agree early: baseline (simple rules), target metric, timeline for experiments.

Final project

Write an ML PRD for a fraud or recommendation feature: problem type, labels and data, metrics and threshold logic, A/B plan, monitoring, model card.

Key takeaways
  • Start from a simple baseline.
  • Agree metrics and costs of errors early.
  • Document with a model card.
Practice: Complete the ML PRD.

Interview prep

15 interview questions with answers

How is ML PM different from regular PM?

Probabilistic outputs, data dependency, metric trade-offs, experimentation and ongoing monitoring/retraining.

Precision vs recall trade-off?

Choose based on the cost of false positives vs false negatives; set thresholds accordingly and validate online.

How do you handle cold start?

Onboarding preferences, popular/trending items, content-based features, and exploration.

What is drift?

Change in input data or relationships over time that degrades model quality; detect via monitoring and retrain.

What goes in an ML PRD?

Problem type, labels/data, metrics and thresholds, baseline, experiment plan, monitoring, rollback, model card.

How do you decide whether ML is the right solution?

Check if rules or a lookup solve most of the problem, whether there is enough quality data and labels, whether wrong predictions are tolerable, and whether value is measurable. Otherwise start without ML.

Precision or recall: how do you choose?

From the cost of each error type. If misses are costly (fraud), favour recall with review steps; if false alarms are costly (blocking customers), favour precision. Pick the threshold with a cost matrix.

What is data leakage?

Using information in training that would not be available at prediction time, which inflates offline results and fails in production.

What is the cold-start problem?

Not having enough data for a new user or item. Solutions include popularity, metadata, onboarding questions and exploration.

Offline metrics improved but the A/B test did not. Why?

Offline data may not reflect new behaviour, there may be latency or edge-case problems, the metric may not match the business goal, or feedback loops and novelty effects are in play.

What is model drift?

Data drift is a change in inputs; concept drift is a change in the relationship between inputs and outcomes. Both reduce performance and need monitoring and retraining.

How do you work with data scientists?

Share the business problem and metric, agree baselines and thresholds, review error analysis together, plan data work early, and make trade-offs explicit.

How would you measure a recommendation system?

Offline NDCG and hit rate, online click-through, add-to-cart, conversion and revenue per user, plus diversity, fairness to sellers and long-term retention as guardrails.

What is a feature store?

A shared system that computes and serves features consistently for training and prediction, avoiding training-serving skew.

How would you handle a model failure in production?

Use a fallback (rules or previous model), alert owners, roll back, analyse root cause, and add tests and monitoring to prevent recurrence.

Advanced AI PM · 13 classes · basic to advanced

AI Governance & Responsible AI

AI governance is the set of policies, reviews and controls that make sure AI is safe, fair, legal and accountable, so teams can ship faster with fewer surprises.

Basic · Class 1

Principles and risks

Know the main responsible-AI principles and risks.

Typical risks: harmful or wrong outputs, bias, privacy leaks, IP/copyright, security (prompt injection), over-reliance, and job or social impact.

AI risk map

RiskExampleTypical control
Bias and unfair outcomesLoan model approves fewer applicants from a regionFairness tests, diverse data, human review
Privacy and data leakageChatbot reveals another customer's detailsAccess controls, redaction, no-training agreements, retention limits
Hallucination and misinformationAssistant invents a refund policyGrounding, citations, evals, disclaimers
SecurityPrompt injection makes an agent send data outInput and output filtering, least-privilege tools, red teaming
Safety and misuseGenerating harmful contentPolicy filters, monitoring, rate limits
IP and copyrightOutput copies protected materialLicensed data, content filters, review
Opacity and accountabilityNo one can explain a decisionLogs, documentation, explainability where needed
Operational and vendorProvider changes a model, quality dropsVersioning, regression evals, exit plans
Key takeaways
  • Principles must turn into checks.
  • List risks per feature.
  • Name an accountable owner.
Practice: List the top 5 risks of an AI hiring-screening feature.

Intermediate · Class 3

AI risk and impact assessment

Assess a feature before launch.

Use evals and red-teaming results as evidence for each mitigation.

Risk tiering example

TierExamplesRequired reviews
HighCredit decisions, hiring, health triage, anything affecting rights or safetyFull impact assessment, legal review, bias testing, human oversight, audit logs, pre-launch sign-off
MediumCustomer-facing chatbots, personalised pricing nudgesRisk review, evals, disclosure, monitoring

Key takeaways
  • Assess before launch, not after incidents.
  • Evidence = evals and red-team results.

Intermediate · Class 4

Policies and documentation

Write the documents governance needs.

  • Company AI use policy (what tools, what data, approvals).
  • Model/system cards: purpose, data, evaluation, limits, contacts.
  • Data protection impact assessment for personal data.
  • User-facing disclosures: "You're chatting with AI", AI-generated labels.
  • Decision logs for high-impact choices.

Documents every AI feature should have

DocumentWhat it contains
Model / system cardPurpose, model and version, data sources, limits, known failure modes, eval results, intended and prohibited use
Data sheetWhere data came from, consent and licence, quality, bias checks, retention
Risk assessmentHazards, likelihood and impact, mitigations, residual risk and owner
DPIA / privacy impactPersonal data used, purpose, necessity, safeguards
Human oversight planWho reviews what, escalation, override powers
Incident runbookHow to detect, contain, communicate, fix and learn
Change logModel and prompt changes with evals and approvals
Key takeaways
  • Document purpose, data, evals and limits.
  • Disclose AI to users.
  • Keep decision logs.
Practice: Draft a 1-page AI use policy for a 50-person startup.
Intermediate · Class 5

Fairness, bias and explainability

Test whether AI treats groups fairly and can explain itself.

Bias enters through data (who is represented), labels (human judgments), features (proxies such as pincode for caste or income) and deployment (who uses the system and how).

Fairness ideaPlain meaningExample check
Demographic paritySimilar positive rates across groupsLoan approval rate by gender and region
Equal opportunitySimilar true positive ratesAmong creditworthy applicants, share approved by group
CalibrationScores mean the same across groupsA 70% risk score reflects 70% observed risk in each group
Error-rate balanceSimilar false positives and negativesFraud flags wrongly raised on one group more often
  • These measures can conflict; choose using the harm, law and context, and document why.
  • Test on slices (language, region, device, gender where lawful and ethical to measure) not only overall accuracy.
  • Explainability: give reasons users can act on ("your income documents were incomplete") and keep logs for audits. Use simple models for high-stakes decisions where possible.
  • Appeal and redress: users should be able to contest and reach a human.
Key takeaways
  • Test performance by slice, not only overall.
  • Fairness measures can conflict; document the choice.
  • Give actionable reasons and a way to appeal.
Practice: Design a fairness test plan for a loan-eligibility model, listing slices, metrics and thresholds.
Intermediate · Class 6

Privacy, security and AI-specific attacks

Protect user data and the AI system itself.

Privacy by design for AI

  • Minimise: send only needed fields to the model; mask PAN, Aadhaar, phone numbers.
  • Purpose limitation: use data only for the stated purpose; get consent for new uses.
  • Vendors: data processing agreements, no training on your data, retention and deletion, location of processing.
  • Rights: access, correction, deletion; can you remove a person from logs, embeddings and fine-tuning data?

AI-specific security threats

ThreatWhat happensDefence
Prompt injectionHidden instructions in a web page or document hijack the modelSeparate instructions from data, filter, least-privilege tools, human approval for risky actions
Data exfiltrationModel leaks secrets or other users' dataAccess controls on retrieval, redaction, output checks
JailbreaksUsers bypass safety rulesLayered filters, monitoring, red teaming
Training data poisoningBad data corrupts a modelSource vetting, review, anomaly detection
Model theft or abuseScraping, high-volume misuseRate limits, auth, monitoring
Supply-chain riskCompromised plugins, models or packagesVendor reviews, pinned versions, scanning
Treat an AI agent like a junior employee with a master key: give it only the access it needs, log everything, and require approval for actions that move money or data.
Key takeaways
  • Minimise and mask data before it reaches the model.
  • Prompt injection is the top new threat for agents.
  • Least privilege and logs for every tool.
Practice: Run a threat model for an AI support agent that can issue refunds.
Advanced · Class 7

Operating governance

Run governance without slowing teams down.

  • Tiered review: light checklist for low-risk features, committee review for high-risk.
  • Incident response: report, triage, rollback, communicate, learn.
  • Audits: periodic eval and bias re-checks, access reviews.
  • Vendor management: data terms, security, model changes.

Governance in the lifecycle

Key takeaways
  • Tier the process by risk.
  • Have an incident playbook.
  • Re-check periodically.
Practice: Design a tiered AI review process for your company.
Advanced · Class 8

Red teaming, evaluation and monitoring for safety

Test for harm before and after launch.

  • Define harms: list what could go wrong for users, the company and third parties (misinformation, harassment, privacy leaks, unsafe advice, discrimination).
  • Build test sets: adversarial prompts, edge cases, multilingual and Hinglish inputs, sensitive topics.
  • Red team: internal and external testers try to make the system fail; record findings and severity.
  • Guardrails: input and output filters, refusal policies, grounding, rate limits, human escalation.
  • Monitor: sampled reviews, user reports, drift in quality, harmful-output rates, complaint themes.
  • Incident response: severity levels, kill switch, owner on call, user communication, regulator notification where required, post-incident review.
MetricExample target
Harmful output rate on red-team setBelow an agreed threshold, with zero critical failures
Refusal correctnessRefuses unsafe requests, answers safe ones
Escalation time for severe incidentsUnder 1 hour to contain
User reports resolvedWithin an agreed time
Key takeaways
  • Test harms before launch and monitor after.
  • Keep a kill switch and an incident runbook.
  • Cover multilingual and adversarial cases.
Practice: Draft a red-team test plan with 20 adversarial prompts for an AI assistant in your domain.
Advanced · Class 9

Vendor due diligence, procurement and third-party AI

Check AI suppliers before you rely on them.

AreaQuestions to ask
DataIs our data used for training? Retention? Location? Deletion on request? Sub-processors?
SecurityCertifications (ISO 27001, SOC 2), pen tests, incident history, access controls
ModelWhich model and version? Change notifications? Deprecation policy? Evaluation reports?
LegalIP indemnity, liability caps, audit rights, compliance with DPDP and other laws
ReliabilitySLA, uptime history, rate limits, support
ExitData export, switching cost, escrow or fallback
Responsible AIPolicies, red-team practice, transparency, content provenance

Create a standard questionnaire, risk-rate each vendor, keep a register of AI tools in use (including shadow AI used by employees) and review annually.

Key takeaways
  • Use a standard vendor questionnaire.
  • Know which AI tools are in use, including unofficial ones.
  • Plan exit before you sign.
Practice: Create an AI vendor due diligence checklist and rate two tools you use.
Advanced · Class 10

Building a responsible-AI programme and culture

Make governance practical and lasting.

  • Principles to practice: turn values (fairness, transparency, privacy, safety, accountability) into checklists, tests and owners.
  • Structure: an AI governance committee for high-risk cases, product-level owners, and a lightweight intake process so teams are not blocked.
  • Policies: acceptable use for employees (what data may go into public AI tools), AI procurement, human oversight, disclosure to users, incident handling.
  • Training: role-based, for PMs, engineers, support and executives.
  • Transparency: tell users when they interact with AI, how their data is used, and how to reach a human.
  • Metrics: percent of AI features with risk assessment, evals, monitoring; open issues by severity; incidents and time to resolve; training completion.
  • Culture: reward people for raising risks; run blameless reviews; make the safe path the easy path.
Good governance speeds teams up by making the rules clear and the reviews predictable. Bad governance is a late-stage veto.
Key takeaways
  • Turn principles into checklists, tests and owners.
  • Keep intake light; reserve deep review for high risk.
  • Measure coverage and incident handling.
Practice: Draft a one-page AI acceptable-use policy for employees.
Advanced · Class 11

Case studies: three governance decisions

Apply governance to practical situations (illustrative).

Case 1: Loan approval model shows regional gap

  • Finding: approval rate is 18 points lower in one region at similar income levels.
  • Investigation: a proxy feature (pincode-based risk score) drives the gap; data coverage is poor there.
  • Actions: remove or adjust the proxy, add alternative data with consent, set fairness thresholds, human review for borderline cases, and document the decision for audit.
  • Monitor: monthly slice metrics; report to the governance committee.

Case 2: Employees paste customer data into a public chatbot

  • Risk: personal data leaves the company; possible DPDP breach.
  • Actions: acceptable-use policy, approved tools with enterprise terms, data loss prevention, training, and logging; provide a safe alternative so people do not use shadow AI.

Case 3: Support bot gives a wrong refund policy

  • Severity: medium; customers affected; brand risk.
  • Response: kill switch for the policy topic, correct the knowledge base, add a citation requirement and an eval for refund questions, notify affected customers, and run a blameless review.
Key takeaways
  • Investigate causes before choosing fixes.
  • Provide safe alternatives to prevent shadow AI.
  • Keep incident response ready.
Practice: Choose a case and write the governance memo: finding, risk, actions, owner, date.
Advanced · Class 12

Interview practice: governance scenario questions

Answer responsible-AI questions clearly.

Q. How would you launch an AI feature responsibly?
Model answer: I would risk-tier it, run an impact assessment, document data and model limits, test fairness and safety with red-team sets, add guardrails, human oversight and disclosure, plan monitoring and an incident runbook, and get the required sign-offs before a staged rollout.
Why it works: It follows the lifecycle.
Q. Regulators ask how your model makes decisions. What do you provide?
Model answer: Model documentation, data sources and quality checks, evaluation and fairness results, human oversight procedures, logs of decisions and changes, and the risk assessment with mitigations.
Why it works: Evidence-based.
Q. How do you balance innovation speed and governance?
Model answer: Use risk-based tiers: lightweight checks for low-risk features, deeper reviews for high-risk, automate checks in pipelines, and make policies clear so teams know what is required.
Why it works: Speed through clarity.
Q. What are the biggest AI risks for a consumer app?
Model answer: Wrong or harmful outputs, privacy leakage, bias, security attacks such as prompt injection, IP issues and over-reliance by users; mitigated through evals, guardrails, access controls, transparency and monitoring.
Why it works: Complete risk map.
Key takeaways
  • Follow the lifecycle: assess, test, guard, monitor, review.
  • Use tiers to keep speed.
  • Prepare evidence.
Practice: Write answers to all four in your own words.
Advanced · Class 13

Final project

Govern a real AI feature.

For an AI feature, produce: risk tier, risk assessment table, mitigations with eval evidence, system card, user disclosure copy, DPDP checklist, incident playbook.

Key takeaways
  • Governance is a product practice.
  • Evidence over promises.
  • Make it lightweight for low risk.
Practice: Complete the governance pack.

Interview prep

15 interview questions with answers

What is responsible AI?

Building AI that is accountable, safe, fair, private and transparent, backed by processes and evidence.

How does the EU AI Act affect products?

Obligations depend on risk tier; high-risk uses like hiring or credit need risk management, data governance, documentation and human oversight.

What does DPDP mean for AI features?

Lawful consent/purpose, minimal data, user rights, security, and care with personal data in prompts and logs.

How do you run a risk assessment?

Describe use, identify risks, rate them, add mitigations with eval evidence, sign off residual risk, monitor.

How do you keep governance fast?

Tiered reviews, templates, automation of checks, clear owners.

What is responsible AI?

Building and operating AI so it is fair, safe, private, transparent and accountable, with controls that match the risk.

What are the EU AI Act's risk tiers?

Unacceptable risk (banned), high risk (strict obligations), limited risk (transparency duties) and minimal risk. Providers of general-purpose models have additional obligations.

How does India's DPDP Act affect AI products?

It requires consent and notice, purpose limitation, data minimisation, security and breach reporting, and gives people rights over their data, which affects training data, logs and retention.

How would you test an AI feature for bias?

Define slices, choose fairness metrics relevant to the harm, compare error rates and outcomes across slices, investigate causes, mitigate, and document.

What is prompt injection and how do you defend against it?

Malicious instructions hidden in content the model reads. Defend with separation of instructions and data, least-privilege tools, filtering and human approval for risky actions.

What is a model card?

A document describing a model's purpose, data, performance, limits and intended use, used for transparency and review.

How do you handle an AI incident?

Detect, contain (kill switch), assess severity, communicate to affected users and regulators if required, fix, and run a blameless review.

What would you ask an AI vendor before signing?

Data use and retention, security certifications, model change policy, IP indemnity, SLAs, exit options and responsible-AI practices.

How do you balance speed and governance?

Risk-tier features, use lightweight checklists for low risk, reserve deep review for high risk, and embed governance in the delivery process.

When should a human stay in the loop?

For decisions affecting rights, money, safety or health, for low-confidence outputs, and for novel or sensitive cases.

Advanced AI PM · 14 classes · basic to advanced

Platform & API Product Management

A platform PM builds products that other teams, developers or partners build on: APIs, SDKs, internal platforms and ecosystems. The users are developers, and the product is how easily they succeed.

Basic · Class 1

Platforms and APIs as products

Understand platform types and users.

Examples: UPI/payment APIs (Razorpay, Stripe), maps APIs, WhatsApp Business API, internal identity or AI platforms, MCP servers that expose your product to AI assistants.

Product types compared

ApplicationPlatform / API
CustomerEnd userDevelopers, partners and the apps they build
ValueSolves a taskEnables others to solve many tasks
GrowthUsers and revenueEcosystem size, integrations, usage volume
RiskUsability, retentionBreaking changes, reliability, trust

Examples: Stripe and Razorpay (payments), Twilio (messaging), Google Maps Platform (location), UPI and ONDC (open networks), Shopify (commerce platform), and AI APIs from model providers.

  • Internal platforms are products too.
  • AI assistants are a new channel (MCP).
Practice: Map the platform users and their jobs for a payments company.
Basic · Class 2

Developer experience (DX)

Make developers successful fast.

  • Time to first successful call (aim for minutes).
  • Clear docs, quickstarts, SDKs, sandbox keys, Postman collections.
  • Helpful errors, status page, changelog, community support.

Developer journey

The key metric is time to first successful call (TTFC). Under 10 minutes is a good target for many APIs. Every extra step (manual approval, unclear docs, missing sandbox) loses developers.

Key takeaways
  • Measure time to first call.
  • Docs and sandbox are the onboarding.
  • Errors should explain the fix.
Practice: Audit a public API's onboarding and list 5 improvements.
Intermediate · Class 3

API design decisions for PMs

Decide what matters in API contracts.

  • Resources and endpoints that match developer jobs; consistent naming.
  • Authentication (API keys, OAuth), permissions and scopes.
  • Versioning and deprecation policy (e.g. 12 months notice).
  • Rate limits and quotas; idempotency keys for payments.
  • Webhooks for events; pagination; error formats.

API design checklist for PMs

TopicDecision and why it matters
Resources and namingUse customer-meaningful nouns (orders, payments); consistent patterns
REST vs GraphQL vs eventsREST is simple and cacheable; GraphQL lets clients ask for exact data; webhooks and events notify of changes
VersioningNever break existing clients; introduce versions (v1, v2) or date-based versions; publish a deprecation policy
IdempotencyAllow safe retries for payments and orders using idempotency keys
Pagination and filteringCursor pagination for large lists
ErrorsConsistent codes, human-readable messages, request IDs
Rate limits and quotasProtect the system; document limits and retry guidance
Auth and scopesAPI keys for simple cases; OAuth 2.0 for user-delegated access; least-privilege scopes
Key takeaways
  • Contracts are promises: version carefully.
  • Rate limits protect reliability.
  • Webhooks make integrations real-time.
Practice: Write the API requirements for a 'refund' endpoint.
Intermediate · Class 4

Ecosystems and partners

Grow a platform through others.

  • Partner tiers, certification, marketplace listing, revenue share.
  • Governance: app review, security, data access rules.

Partner programme tiers

TierRequirementsBenefits
RegisteredSign up, accept termsDocs, sandbox, community
CertifiedPass quality and security checksListing, badge, support
StrategicRevenue or usage thresholds, joint roadmapCo-marketing, early access, account manager
Key takeaways
  • Platforms grow through network effects.
  • Partners need clear rules and incentives.
  • Review apps for security.
Practice: Design a partner program for a SaaS marketplace.
Intermediate · Class 5

API lifecycle, versioning and deprecation

Evolve APIs without breaking the apps that depend on them.

  • Contract first: design using OpenAPI; review with real developers before building.
  • Breaking vs non-breaking: adding optional fields is usually safe; removing or renaming fields, changing types or behaviour is breaking.
  • Deprecation policy: announce early (6 to 12 months for critical APIs), publish migration guides, add warning headers, email active users, track usage of old versions, sunset only when usage is low or after contacting the remaining users.
  • Changelog and status: a public changelog and a status page build trust.
  • SDKs and tooling: official SDKs in top languages, Postman collections, CLI, and code samples that stay tested.
  • Backwards compatibility tests: automated contract tests so a release cannot break clients silently.
For a platform, a breaking change you did not announce can cost more trust than a bug. Treat deprecation as a product launch with its own plan.
Key takeaways
  • Design contract-first and with developers.
  • Deprecate with long notice and migration help.
  • Automate compatibility tests.
Practice: Write a deprecation plan for an API field you want to remove.
Intermediate · Class 6

Developer portal, documentation and community

Make developers successful without talking to you.

ElementWhat good looks like
QuickstartWorking code in 5 minutes, copy-paste, in the top 3 languages
Reference docsEvery endpoint with examples, errors, limits and try-it console
Guides and use casesTask-based tutorials (accept a payment, send a message)
Sandbox and test dataSafe environment with fake data and test keys
Search and navigationFast search, versioned docs, copy buttons
Support and communityForum, Discord or Slack, office hours, response-time targets
Status and changelogIncidents, maintenance, release notes
AnalyticsDocs page feedback, search terms with no results, drop-off in quickstart

Docs are product. Assign owners, test them with new developers, and measure time to first call, quickstart completion, docs satisfaction and support tickets per 1,000 developers.

Key takeaways
  • Quickstart in minutes, in popular languages.
  • Sandbox and test data are essential.
  • Measure the docs funnel.
Practice: Test your favourite API's quickstart as a new developer and list the three biggest frictions.
Intermediate · Class 7

API security, authentication and compliance

Protect users, data and the platform.

TopicPlain meaningPM decision
API keysA secret string identifying the appRotation, scopes, per-environment keys
OAuth 2.0Users grant apps limited access without sharing passwordsWhich scopes? Consent screens and review of apps
JWT and tokensSigned proof of identity and permissions with expiryToken lifetime vs usability
Rate limiting and quotasCaps per key or userFair use, abuse protection, paid tiers
Webhook signaturesProve the message came from youDocumentation and retry rules
Data protectionEncryption, minimisation, retentionDPDP, GDPR, PCI-DSS, RBI rules
Audit logsWho did what and whenCustomer-visible logs for enterprise
App reviewCheck partner apps before they get sensitive scopesReview criteria and timelines
Principle: least privilege. Give each app only the access it needs, make it visible to users, and make it easy to revoke.
Key takeaways
  • Use OAuth and scopes for user data.
  • Rate limit and sign webhooks.
  • Review partner apps before granting sensitive access.
Practice: Define scopes and a review process for an app marketplace that can read customer orders.

Platform metrics

Measure platform health.

MetricWhy

Platform metrics tree

LayerMetrics

Advanced · Class 9

Platform business models and network effects

Choose how a platform earns and grows.

ModelHow it earnsExampleWatch out for
Usage-basedPer call, message or transactionPayments, SMS, maps, AI APIsUnpredictable bills; margin on usage
Tiered subscriptionPlan with included usageDeveloper toolsPlan boundaries confuse
Revenue share / take ratePercentage of partner revenueMarketplaces and app storesPartners resent high rates
Freemium plus enterpriseFree to start, paid for scale and supportMany API productsCost of free usage
Data / network valueValue rises as more joinOpen networks like UPI and ONDCNeeds governance and neutrality

Network effects

  • Direct: more users make the product more valuable for each user.
  • Two-sided: more developers attract more users and vice versa; solve the "chicken and egg" by subsidising one side or seeding with your own apps.
  • Data effects: usage improves the platform (fraud models, routing).
  • Multi-homing: developers may use competing platforms; lower switching for them means you must keep quality and economics strong.
Key takeaways
  • Match pricing to cost and value.
  • Solve the chicken-and-egg problem on purpose.
  • Watch multi-homing and take-rate tension.
Practice: Choose a business model for a delivery-logistics API and justify it.
Advanced · Class 10

Internal platforms and platform engineering

Treat internal tools as products for internal customers.

  • Platform as a product: internal teams are your customers; run discovery, roadmap, onboarding and support.
  • Golden paths: opinionated, well-supported ways to build, test, deploy and monitor, so teams get speed and safety by default.
  • Self-service: developers provision what they need (environments, databases, pipelines) without tickets.
  • Metrics: adoption of the platform, lead time for changes, deployment frequency, change failure rate and time to restore (DORA), developer satisfaction, onboarding time for new engineers.
  • Build vs buy vs adopt open source: consider total cost, differentiation, skills and risk.
  • AI platforms: shared model gateway (routing, keys, logging, cost caps), evaluation service, vector store, prompt library, guardrails and monitoring, so product teams do not rebuild them.
Anti-patternFix
Platform team builds what it finds interestingDiscovery with internal users; publish roadmap
Mandating use with no valueMake it the easiest path; measure adoption
No support modelOffice hours, SLAs, docs
Too many optionsGolden paths and defaults
Key takeaways
  • Treat internal users as customers.
  • Golden paths and self-service drive adoption.
  • Measure with DORA and developer satisfaction.
Practice: Define the roadmap and metrics for an internal AI model gateway.
Advanced · Class 11

Case studies: payments, communications and open networks

Learn what great platforms do.

Payments APIs (Stripe, Razorpay)

They won on developer experience: clean docs, copy-paste quickstarts, test mode, clear error messages, webhooks with signatures and strong reliability. Lesson: reduce time to first transaction and keep the surface area simple.

Communications APIs (Twilio-style)

Usage-based pricing that scales from a hobby project to an enterprise, strong SDKs and tutorials, and expansion across channels (SMS, voice, WhatsApp, email). Lesson: start small with a clear use case, then expand through adjacent APIs.

Open networks (UPI, ONDC)

UPI created an interoperable payments network with open specifications used by many apps; ONDC applies a similar idea to commerce. Lesson: neutral rules, strong governance and low switching costs can create huge ecosystems, but require careful standards, dispute handling and fair economics.

AI APIs

Model APIs compete on quality, price, latency and reliability, and keep adding tools (function calling, batch, caching). Lesson: abstract providers behind a gateway and plan for changes in pricing, limits and model versions.

Key takeaways
  • Developer experience is the moat for API products.
  • Start with one clear use case, then expand.
  • Open networks need governance as much as technology.
Practice: Write a teardown of one API product using the developer funnel and the metrics tree.
Advanced · Class 12

Case studies: three platform decisions

Practise platform product thinking (illustrative).

Case 1: A payments API has a 40-minute time to first call

  • Diagnosis: manual account approval, long docs, no sandbox keys at sign-up.
  • Actions: instant test keys, a 5-minute quickstart, a Postman collection, and sample apps; move approvals to when going live.
  • Target: TTFC under 10 minutes; activation up 30%.

Case 2: Must remove an old field used by 5% of integrations

  • Announce 9 months ahead, add warnings, provide a migration guide and script, contact top 20 users personally, track usage weekly, and delay sunset if critical customers have not migrated.

Case 3: Internal AI gateway for 12 product teams

  • Problems: duplicated integrations, no cost visibility, inconsistent safety.
  • Platform offers: single API for models, keys per team, caching, rate limits, logging, guardrails, evals and a prompt library.
  • Metrics: teams onboarded, time to add a feature, cost per team, incidents, developer satisfaction.
Key takeaways
  • Measure and fix the developer funnel.
  • Treat deprecation as a launch.
  • Internal platforms need product management too.
Practice: Choose a case and write the roadmap for the next 90 days.
Advanced · Class 13

Interview practice: platform and API scenario questions

Answer platform PM questions with structure.

Q. How would you improve the developer experience of an API?
Model answer: I would measure the developer funnel, find drop-offs, reduce time to first call with instant sandbox keys and a short quickstart, improve error messages and docs, add SDKs and samples, and build support and community channels. I would track TTFC, activation, tickets and developer NPS.
Why it works: Funnel thinking plus metrics.
Q. How do you prioritise between new features and stability?
Model answer: Stability and compatibility are the product for a platform. I would use error budgets and SLOs to decide, protect a share of capacity for reliability and debt, and prioritise features by partner impact and ecosystem growth.
Why it works: Shows platform-specific trade-offs.
Q. How would you price a new API?
Model answer: Use usage-based pricing linked to the value metric with a free tier for experimentation, volume tiers and enterprise contracts. Validate with early customers and watch margin on usage.
Why it works: Ties pricing to value metric.
Q. How do you decide what to open to third parties?
Model answer: Start with capabilities that create partner value and low risk, use scoped access and app review, learn from a small beta group, and expand with strong governance.
Why it works: Controlled openness.
Key takeaways
  • Use funnels, SLOs and value metrics.
  • Open capabilities gradually.
  • Communicate changes early.
Practice: Write your own answers and metrics for each.
Advanced · Class 14

AI platforms and final project

Apply platform thinking to AI.

  • Internal AI platforms: shared model access, evals, guardrails, prompt/skill libraries, cost tracking.
  • Exposing your product via MCP so AI assistants can use it.

Final project

Write a platform PRD for a public API or internal AI platform: users, developer journey, API requirements, limits and versioning, partner rules, metrics.

Key takeaways
  • AI platforms centralise models, evals and guardrails.
  • MCP is a new distribution channel.
  • Treat developers like customers.
Practice: Complete the platform PRD.

Interview prep

14 interview questions with answers

What does a platform PM do?

Builds products other teams or developers build on, optimising developer success, reliability and ecosystem growth.

Key DX metric?

Time to first successful API call, plus time to production.

How do you version an API?

Explicit versions, backward compatibility, deprecation notices, migration guides and changelogs.

Platform metrics?

Active developers/apps, success rate, latency, calls, revenue, support friction.

What is an AI platform team?

Provides shared model access, evals, guardrails, prompt/skill libraries and cost controls to product teams.

What does a platform PM do differently from an app PM?

Serves developers and partners, focuses on capabilities, stability, developer experience, ecosystem health and versioning, and measures adoption, usage and reliability rather than only end-user features.

How do you measure developer experience?

Time to first successful call, quickstart completion, docs satisfaction, support tickets per developer, developer NPS and activation rate.

How do you handle breaking changes?

Avoid them; if needed use versioning, long deprecation notice, migration guides, usage tracking and direct outreach to affected developers.

REST or GraphQL?

REST is simple, cacheable and widely understood; GraphQL fits complex client data needs. Many platforms offer REST with webhooks and add GraphQL where the use case demands.

What is idempotency in APIs?

Making repeated requests safe so a retry does not create duplicates, typically using an idempotency key.

How would you price an API?

Usage-based or tiered, tied to the value metric (messages, calls, transactions), with a free tier for developers and enterprise contracts for scale.

How do you solve the chicken-and-egg problem for a platform?

Seed with first-party apps, subsidise one side, target a narrow high-value segment first, and make joining easy.

What are DORA metrics?

Deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore service; used to measure engineering delivery performance.

How would you run a partner programme?

Define tiers, certification, technical and security requirements, benefits, support and review processes, and measure partner-sourced revenue and satisfaction.

Advanced AI PM · 12 classes · basic to advanced

Product Operations

Product operations is the function that makes product teams run smoothly at scale: shared processes, tools, data and insight pipelines, so PMs spend time on decisions instead of admin.

Basic · Class 1

What product ops is

Know the scope and value of product ops.

Common in companies with 10+ PMs; in smaller teams PMs do it themselves.

What product ops does, by stage of company

StageTypical teamFocus
Startup (under 10 PMs)PMs do it themselves; maybe one ops hireSimple rituals, a single source of truth
Scale-up (10 to 50 PMs)1 to 3 product opsPlanning cadence, tooling, launches, data
Enterprise (50+)A product operations teamGovernance, portfolio view, analytics, enablement, vendor management

Product ops is not a project manager, a PM's assistant or a bureaucracy team. It exists so product managers spend more time with customers and decisions and less on admin.

Key takeaways
  • Product ops removes friction.
  • Four pillars: data, process, tools, enablement.
  • Scale matters.

Design lightweight rhythms.

Each ritual needs an owner, inputs, outputs and a template; cut rituals that don't change decisions.

A sample quarterly rhythm

WhenRitualInputOutputOwner
Weeks -4 to -2Quarterly planningStrategy, metrics, customer insightsPriorities and OKRsHead of product + product ops
WeeklyProduct staffDashboard, blockersDecisions and actionsProduct lead
Every 2 weeksRoadmap reviewDelivery status, risksUpdated roadmapPM + engineering lead

Intermediate · Class 3

Tools and data

Run the product tool stack and metrics.

  • Single source of truth for roadmap and feedback (Productboard, Jira Product Discovery, Notion).
  • Metrics definitions and dashboards (a metrics dictionary).
  • Clean taxonomy: product areas, customer segments, tags.
  • Tool consolidation and access hygiene.

A tool stack that works (examples)

NeedExamplesTip
Roadmap and strategyProductboard, Aha!, Jira Product Discovery, NotionOne roadmap, different views for execs and teams
Feedback and insightsProductboard, Dovetail, Enterpret, AirtableTag consistently; link feedback to opportunities
AnalyticsMixpanel, Amplitude, GA4, PostHogCommon event taxonomy and tracking plan
ExperimentationOptimizely, Statsig, GrowthBook, in-houseCentral guardrails and a registry of tests
Docs and knowledgeNotion, Confluence, Google DocsTemplates and a single index
DeliveryJira, Linear, Azure DevOpsLink tickets to goals and metrics

Tracking plan (a product ops staple)

A shared sheet listing every event: name, trigger, properties, owner, and the question it answers. Example: checkout_started (cart_value, items, device), used for the funnel from product page to payment. Without it, dashboards disagree and trust in data collapses.

Key takeaways
  • One source of truth per object.
  • A metrics dictionary prevents arguments.
  • Taxonomy makes insights searchable.
Practice: Draft a metrics dictionary with 8 metrics.
Intermediate · Class 4

Customer-insight pipelines

Turn feedback into prioritised insights.

A feedback taxonomy

LevelExample tags
Product areaSearch, Checkout, Payments, Onboarding, Support
TypeBug, usability, missing feature, pricing, performance, praise
SegmentSMB, enterprise, new user, power user, region
Severity / valueBlocker, major, minor; revenue at risk
SourceSupport, sales call, NPS, review, interview, social

Report monthly: top 10 themes, trend, revenue linked, and what was done. Close the loop by telling customers when you ship what they asked for.

Key takeaways
  • AI can tag and cluster feedback at scale.
  • Link insights to opportunities and revenue.
  • Close the loop with customers.
Practice: Build a feedback-tagging taxonomy and test it on 30 items with AI.
Intermediate · Class 5

Planning, OKRs and roadmap operations

Run a planning process that people trust.

Product ops makes planning predictable: same inputs, same calendar, clear outputs.

OKRs for product teams (example)

ObjectiveKey results
Make first purchase easier for new usersIncrease first-order conversion from 22% to 28%; cut median checkout time from 95 s to 60 s; keep payment success at or above 97%
Reduce support load from order issuesReduce 'where is my order' contacts per 100 orders from 6 to 4; launch proactive delay alerts to 100% of orders

Prioritisation criteria

Agree the criteria once: impact on the goal, reach, confidence, effort, strategic fit, risk. Use a simple score (RICE or weighted) as an input, never as an automatic decision.

Roadmap hygiene

  • Roadmaps show outcomes and themes for the next 1 to 2 quarters, not dates for every feature.
  • Keep three views: exec (themes and outcomes), team (epics and dependencies), customer-facing (what is coming, with no hard dates).
  • Publish changes and the reason for them.
Key takeaways
  • Same inputs, same calendar, clear outputs.
  • OKRs: outcomes with measurable key results.
  • Roadmaps show outcomes, not a feature-date list.
Practice: Write one objective with three key results for your product and draft the exec and team roadmap views.
Intermediate · Class 6

Data, analytics and experimentation operations

Give product teams trustworthy numbers and a safe way to test.

The data foundation

  • Metrics dictionary: one definition for each metric (active user, conversion, retention) with formula, source and owner.
  • Tracking plan and QA: events defined before build and tested before release.
  • Dashboards: a company KPI dashboard, a product-area dashboard for each team, and a launch dashboard template.
  • Self-serve access: training so PMs can query basic questions without waiting for analysts.

Experiment operations

StepProduct ops role
Idea and hypothesisProvide template: problem, change, metric, guardrails
DesignCheck sample size, duration, segments, conflicts with other tests
RunMonitor sample ratio mismatch and guardrails
Read-outStandard report: effect, confidence interval, decision
ArchiveExperiment registry so learnings are searchable
Common failures: metrics defined differently by different teams, experiments that overlap, peeking at results early, and no record of past learnings.
Key takeaways
  • A metrics dictionary prevents arguments.
  • Plan events before building.
  • Run experiments with templates, checks and an archive.
Practice: Draft a metrics dictionary for five core metrics and a tracking plan for one flow.
Advanced · Class 7

Launch management and governance

Make launches predictable.

  • Launch tiers (big, medium, small) with checklists.
  • Go/no-go reviews with evals, support readiness, docs, legal.
  • Release notes and internal enablement; post-launch reviews.

Launch tiers and checklist

TierExampleRequirements
Tier 1 (major)New product, pricing change, big redesignFull plan: GTM, legal, support training, press, exec review, rollback plan
Tier 2 (medium)Significant featureRelease notes, enablement, help articles, metrics dashboard
Tier 3 (small)Minor improvementChangelog entry, owner sign-off
Key takeaways
  • Tier launches by impact.
  • Checklists and go/no-go.
  • Post-launch review every time.
Practice: Create a tiered launch checklist.
Advanced · Class 8

Enablement, documentation and cross-functional operations

Make sure sales, support and marketing can sell and support what is shipped.

  • Enablement kit per launch: one-page summary, who it is for, demo video, FAQ, pricing and packaging rules, objection handling, known issues, escalation path.
  • Release notes and changelog: customer-facing language; internal notes for support and sales.
  • Training: short sessions plus recorded demos; test understanding with a quiz.
  • Documentation standards: PRD template, decision log, product glossary, onboarding for new PMs.
  • Customer advisory boards and beta programs: recruit, run, summarise and feed insights back.
  • Vendor and tool management: licences, security reviews, renewals, adoption tracking.
AudienceNeedsFormat
SalesWhy customers buy, pricing, competitorsBattlecard, demo, talk track
Customer supportHow it works, known issues, escalationHelp article, internal FAQ, macros
MarketingPositioning, proof points, launch assetsMessaging doc, case study
ExecutivesOutcome and riskOne-slide summary and dashboard
Key takeaways
  • Enablement is part of the launch, not an afterthought.
  • Write for each audience's decision.
  • Keep documentation standards simple and searchable.
Practice: Create an enablement kit outline for your next feature launch.
Advanced · Class 9

Measuring product ops and building the function

Show the value of product ops and grow it sensibly.

MetricWhat it shows
Time from idea to decisionPlanning efficiency
Launch readiness score and on-time rateLaunch quality
PM time on admin vs customers (survey)Productivity
Data trust score (survey) and metric disputesData reliability
Feedback coverage and closed-loop rateCustomer voice
Experiment velocity and learning rateTesting maturity
Stakeholder satisfactionAlignment

Building a product ops function

  1. Diagnose: interview PMs and partners; list top 10 pains.
  2. Start small: pick 2 or 3 fixes (planning calendar, feedback taxonomy, launch checklist).
  3. Standardise lightly: templates and tools, not heavy process.
  4. Automate: reports, notes, tagging, status updates (with AI where safe).
  5. Report impact: time saved, decisions sped up, quality improved.

Career and skills

Strong product ops professionals combine process design, data fluency, communication, tools knowledge and influence without authority. Paths include Product Ops Manager, Head of Product Operations, Product Manager, Chief of Staff or Program roles.

Key takeaways
  • Measure decisions, speed and trust, not activity.
  • Start with 2 to 3 high-value fixes.
  • Product ops is influence plus systems.
Practice: Define 5 metrics and a 90-day plan to start a product ops function.
Advanced · Class 10

Case studies: three product ops improvements

See how small systems fix big frictions (illustrative).

Case 1: Planning takes six weeks and nobody trusts the roadmap

  • Diagnosis: different templates, inputs arrive late, priorities argued from scratch.
  • Actions: a single planning calendar, one template, shared scoring criteria, a pre-read, and a decision log.
  • Result target: planning in three weeks; roadmap changes explained in the log.

Case 2: Feedback is everywhere and unused

  • Create one intake (form plus integrations), tag with the taxonomy, link to accounts and revenue, publish a monthly top-10 themes report and close the loop.
  • Measure: share of shipped features linked to feedback, response time to customers.

Case 3: Launches surprise sales and support

  • Introduce launch tiers, a checklist, an enablement kit and a go/no-go meeting; set a rule that no launch goes out without a support FAQ.
  • Measure: support tickets in launch week, sales readiness score, post-launch review completion.
Key takeaways
  • Diagnose the pain, then standardise lightly.
  • Make feedback usable and traceable.
  • Launch readiness protects customers.
Practice: Pick a pain in your team and write the diagnosis, actions and measure.
Advanced · Class 11

Interview practice: product operations scenario questions

Answer product ops questions with practical detail.

Q. What would you do in your first 60 days as product ops manager?
Model answer: Interview PMs, designers, engineers and stakeholders; map current processes and tools; list the top 10 pains; pick two or three quick fixes (for example a planning calendar and feedback taxonomy); establish baseline metrics; and share a 90-day plan with owners.
Why it works: Listening, prioritising, measuring.
Q. How do you improve data trust?
Model answer: Create a metrics dictionary, a tracking plan with QA, a single source of truth for dashboards, ownership for each metric and a process for resolving disputes.
Why it works: Systems for data quality.
Q. PMs say process slows them. What do you do?
Model answer: Review each ritual's value; remove or shorten those that do not change decisions; automate reporting; keep templates simple; ask PMs to co-design changes.
Why it works: Empathy plus pruning.
Q. How do you measure the impact of product ops?
Model answer: Time to decision, launch readiness and incident rates, PM time on admin from surveys, data trust scores, feedback closure rate and stakeholder satisfaction.
Why it works: Outcome-focused metrics.
Key takeaways
  • Start with diagnosis and quick fixes.
  • Measure value, not activity.
  • Co-design with PMs.
Practice: Write your 60-day plan in one page.
Advanced · Class 12

AI in product ops and final project

Automate product ops with AI.

  • AI skills for weekly reports, release notes, insight synthesis, meeting notes.
  • Agents that keep Jira and docs in sync (with approvals).
  • Dashboards with AI summaries.

Final project

Design a product-ops toolkit for a 10-PM team: operating rhythm, templates, metrics dictionary, insight pipeline, launch tiers, and 3 AI automations.

Key takeaways
  • Automate reporting and synthesis.
  • Keep humans on decisions.
  • Measure time saved for PMs.

Interview prep

12 interview questions with answers

What is product ops?

A function that scales product teams through data, process, tools and enablement.

When do you need it?

When PM count grows and inconsistency, admin load and scattered data slow decisions.

How do you build an insight pipeline?

Collect from all channels, tag and dedupe (AI-assisted), link to opportunities, quantify, share, close the loop.

How does AI change product ops?

Automates synthesis, reports, release notes and tool hygiene; humans keep decisions.

What does a product operations team do?

It runs the systems around product work: planning, data and analytics, feedback, tooling, launches and enablement, so PMs can focus on customers and decisions.

How is product ops different from a program manager?

Program managers deliver specific cross-team programs. Product ops owns repeatable product systems and standards across the organisation.

How do you decide which ritual to remove?

Ask which decisions it changes. If skipping it changes no decision, shorten or remove it.

What is a tracking plan?

A shared definition of every analytics event, its trigger, properties and owner, so data is consistent and trusted.

How would you build a feedback pipeline?

Collect from support, sales, reviews and interviews, tag with a consistent taxonomy, link to opportunities and revenue, review monthly, and close the loop with customers.

How do you run a successful launch?

Tier the launch, set a checklist, enable sales and support, define metrics, run go/no-go, monitor, and hold a post-launch review.

How would you measure the success of product ops?

Time to decision, launch readiness, data trust, feedback loop closure, experiment velocity, and PM and stakeholder satisfaction.

How do you introduce process without creating bureaucracy?

Start with the biggest pains, keep templates light, involve PMs in design, measure value, and remove what does not help.

Multimodal AI understands and generates more than text: images, audio and video. It powers features like reading invoices from photos, voice assistants, product images and video explainers, along with new risks like deepfakes.

Basic · Class 2

Vision understanding use cases

Use AI to read and interpret images.

  • OCR of invoices, IDs (with consent), forms; handwritten notes.
  • Chart and screenshot understanding; UI review.
  • Quality inspection (manufacturing), crop disease, damage assessment (insurance).
  • Accessibility: describing images for visually impaired users.

Document AI pipeline

  • Measure field-level accuracy (invoice number, date, amount), not just overall text accuracy.
  • Use confidence thresholds: auto-accept high confidence; route low confidence to people.
  • Cross-check totals and dates with business rules (tax = rate x amount).
Key takeaways
  • Vision unlocks offline-to-digital workflows.
  • Mask personal data.
  • Measure accuracy on your own images.
Practice: Design an AI feature that reads shop receipts for expense tracking.
Basic · Class 3

How multimodal AI works (without the maths)

Understand the building blocks so you can reason about capabilities and limits.

  • Embeddings: an image of a red kurta and the words 'red kurta' map to nearby points. Models such as CLIP learn this alignment, which powers image search.
  • Vision-language models: read images and answer questions about them; strong at charts and documents, weaker at precise counting or tiny details.
  • Diffusion models: generate images by starting with noise and removing it step by step following a text prompt.
  • Speech models: speech-to-text (ASR) turns audio into text; text-to-speech (TTS) turns text into audio; voice cloning copies a voice from a sample.
  • Video: treated as sequences of frames plus audio; generation is expensive and improving fast.
Limits to remember: models can misread blurry images, miss small text, hallucinate details, mishandle unusual accents, and show bias. Always test on your own data.
Key takeaways
  • Embeddings link different modalities.
  • Vision models understand; diffusion models generate.
  • Test limits on your own data.
Practice: Explain to a colleague, in 5 sentences, how a photo search for 'blue formal shirt' works.
Intermediate · Class 4

Image generation in products

Use generative images responsibly.

Tools: Midjourney, Adobe Firefly, Ideogram, Leonardo, DALL·E, Imagen, Canva AI. Use cases: ads, product mock-ups, thumbnails, illustrations.

Image generation workflow for a retail catalogue

StepDetail
BriefProduct, angle, background, lighting, brand colours, what must not change
GenerateUse product photos as reference to keep the real item accurate
ReviewCheck logos, text, hands, proportions; reject images that misrepresent the product
EditInpainting, background swap, resizing
Label and publishDisclose AI-generated imagery where policy or law requires; keep source files
Key takeaways
  • Keep brand rules in the brief.
  • Human review before publishing.
  • Prefer tools with clear commercial-use terms.

Intermediate · Class 5

Voice and video

Build with speech and video AI.

  • Speech-to-text and text-to-speech in many Indian languages; voice agents (see Voice Agents lesson).
  • Video: AI summaries and search of recordings; avatar and generative video tools (Runway, Veo, Sora, HeyGen, Synthesia) for explainers.
  • Latency, accents, background noise and cost are key constraints.

Advanced · Class 8

Rights, safety, deepfakes and labelling

Manage the risks of AI media.

  • Copyright and licences: check tool terms for commercial use; avoid copying artists or brands.
  • Consent for faces and voices; never clone voices without permission.
  • Label AI-generated media; content credentials (C2PA) and watermarking.
  • Moderation of user-generated AI media; follow Indian advisories on deepfakes.

Risk map for AI media

RiskExampleControl
CopyrightOutput resembles a protected workLicensed tools, reference checks, avoid 'in the style of living artist' prompts
Likeness and voice rightsCloned celebrity voice in an adWritten consent, contracts, blocklists
Deepfakes and fraudFake CEO video asks for paymentVerification procedures, provenance, detection
MisinformationFake news imagesLabelling, review, platform policy
PrivacyFaces and voices are biometric-like dataConsent, minimisation, retention limits
BiasStereotyped generationsPrompt guidelines, review, testing
Key takeaways
  • Consent for likeness and voice.
  • Label AI media.
  • Check commercial-use rights.
