Advanced · Class 9

Multimodal search, RAG and recommendations

Search across text, images and video.

  • Visual search: snap a photo, find similar products ("shop the look").
  • Video search: find the moment in a lecture or meeting where a topic is discussed (transcribe, split into segments, embed).
  • Multimodal RAG: answer questions using documents with images and tables (charts, scanned forms) by extracting text and also keeping images for vision models.
  • Hybrid ranking: combine similarity with business rules (stock, margin, delivery).
  • Evaluation: relevance judgments by humans, click-through and conversion, zero-result rate, latency.
ChallengeMitigation
Embedding drift when models changeRe-index and version embeddings
Costly indexing of large mediaSample frames, batch processing, tiered storage
Privacy of facesAvoid face recognition unless lawful and consented
Bias in visual similarityAudit results across skin tones, body types, regions
Key takeaways
  • Embed everything into one searchable space.
  • Combine similarity with business rules.
  • Audit for privacy and bias.
Practice: Design a 'shop the look' feature, its pipeline and its metrics.
Advanced · Class 10

Evaluating multimodal quality, safety and cost

Measure what matters before and after launch.

ModalityQuality metricsSafety checks
OCR / document AIField accuracy, exact-match rate, straight-through ratePII masking, access control
Vision Q&AAccuracy on labelled images, hallucination rateUnsafe image detection, privacy blur
SpeechWER, intent success, call completionConsent, DND, abusive-content handling
Image generationPrompt adherence, brand score, human preferenceNSFW, copyright, likeness filters
VideoRealism, sync, user comprehensionDeepfake policy, labelling
  • Golden sets for each modality with edge cases (blurry, low light, accents, noise, tilted forms).
  • Latency and cost budgets per request; use smaller models and caching where possible.
  • Monitoring: sample outputs weekly, track drift (new camera types, new accents), track complaints and escalations.
Key takeaways
  • Build golden sets per modality.
  • Budget latency and cost.
  • Monitor drift and complaints.
Practice: Create an evaluation plan for an invoice-reading feature with thresholds.
Advanced · Class 11

Law, ethics and provenance for AI media in India and globally

Handle rights, consent, disclosure and deepfakes responsibly.

  • Copyright: rules on training data and outputs are evolving and differ by country; use tools with clear commercial terms, keep records of prompts and sources, avoid imitating specific artists or brands.
  • Personality and likeness rights: faces and voices of real people need consent; courts in India have protected celebrity personality rights against unauthorised AI use.
  • Deepfake rules: India's IT Rules and government advisories require platforms to act on deepfakes and encourage labelling of synthetic content; check current requirements.
  • Data protection: biometrics-like data (faces, voiceprints) need consent, purpose limitation and strong security under the DPDP Act.
  • Provenance: content credentials (C2PA) and watermarks help show where media came from; add visible labels where appropriate.
  • Advertising rules: disclose AI use where it could mislead; follow ASCI guidance.
Policy itemExample rule
DisclosureLabel AI-generated images and videos in marketing and news-like contexts
ConsentWritten consent for any real person's face or voice
ProhibitedSexual, deceptive political, impersonation and child-safety violations
ReviewHuman review before publishing sensitive categories
IncidentTakedown process and owner within 24 hours
Not legal advice: consult counsel for your markets, and review rules regularly.
Key takeaways
  • Get consent for faces and voices.
  • Label synthetic media and keep provenance.
  • Write a clear AI media policy with owners.
Practice: Draft an AI media policy page for your team with five rules and an incident process.
Advanced · Class 12

Case studies: three multimodal features

Walk through realistic product designs (illustrative).

Case 1: Expense receipts from photos

  1. Flow: photo → quality check → OCR + AI extraction (vendor, date, amount, tax) → validation → user confirms → expense created.
  2. Accuracy plan: test 500 real receipts; target 95% field accuracy on amount and date; below threshold goes to review.
  3. Cost: Rs 0.40 per receipt vs Rs 12 manual entry.
  4. Risks: blurry photos, handwritten receipts, duplicates (use hash and amount-date check).

Case 2: Hindi voice assistant for appointment booking

  1. Pipeline: telephony → ASR (Hindi/English) → intent and slots → availability API → TTS confirmation → SMS.
  2. Targets: intent success 85%, latency under 1.2 seconds, escalation to a human below 70% confidence.
  3. Compliance: disclose AI, record with consent, respect DND.

Case 3: AI product images for a fashion catalogue

  1. Use real garment photos on generated backgrounds; keep colour and fit accurate.
  2. Human review of 10% sample plus automated colour-difference checks; A/B test conversion and returns.
  3. Disclose AI imagery; keep source files; avoid generating models that look like real people without consent.
Key takeaways
  • Define accuracy per field and per language.
  • Plan human review for low confidence.
  • Test business impact, including returns.
Practice: Choose a case and write targets, risks and monitoring.
Advanced · Class 13

Interview practice: multimodal scenario questions

Answer multimodal product questions.

Q. How would you build a feature that reads Aadhaar or PAN cards from photos?
Model answer: I would treat it as sensitive: get consent, mask data, use secure storage, run quality checks, extract with OCR and validate formats and checksums, route low confidence to manual review, minimise retention, and comply with KYC rules. I would measure field accuracy, completion rate and time.
Why it works: Privacy-first design.
Q. How do you evaluate a voice assistant?
Model answer: Use word error rate on real audio, intent success, task completion, latency, escalation and satisfaction, tested across accents and noise.
Why it works: Complete metrics.
Q. What are the risks of AI-generated product photos?
Model answer: Misrepresenting the product, brand and copyright issues, bias, regulation and customer trust; mitigate with real references, reviews, labels and return-rate monitoring.
Why it works: Risk and mitigation.
Q. How do you reduce the cost of video features?
Model answer: Sample frames, transcribe once and reuse, cache, use smaller models, batch processing, limit resolution and length, and tier by value.
Why it works: Cost levers.
Key takeaways
  • Treat sensitive images and voices carefully.
  • Measure per modality.
  • Control costs with sampling and caching.
Practice: Write your answer to the KYC photo question with a compliance checklist.

Ship a multimodal feature.

Design a multimodal feature (photo receipts, voice ordering, or video course summaries): user flow, model/tool choice, accuracy eval on 30 samples, privacy and consent, labelling, cost estimate.

Interview prep

13 interview questions with answers

What is multimodal AI?

Models that understand and/or generate several types of data: text, images, audio and video.

A good vision use case?

Reading receipts or forms from photos to remove manual entry, with accuracy checks and privacy.

Risks of AI media?

Copyright, consent for likeness and voice, deepfakes, misinformation; mitigate with consent, labelling, C2PA and moderation.

Why voice in India?

Many users prefer speaking, many languages and literacy levels; voice widens access.

What is multimodal AI?

AI that can process or generate more than one type of data, such as text, images, audio and video, often in a single model.

Where does vision AI add the most business value?

Where manual reading of images and documents is frequent: invoices, KYC, forms, quality inspection and claims, with confidence thresholds and human review for exceptions.

How do you evaluate a document AI feature?

Field-level accuracy on a labelled set, straight-through processing rate, error types, cost per document and time saved, with edge cases like blurry photos and handwriting.

What is word error rate?

A speech recognition metric: the share of words that are wrong (substitutions, deletions, insertions) compared with a reference transcript.

What makes voice agents feel natural?

Low latency (about one second), interruption handling, clear voices, accurate recognition of accents and names, and graceful recovery.

What are the main risks of AI-generated media?

Copyright, likeness and consent, deepfakes and fraud, misinformation, privacy and bias; mitigate with consent, labelling, provenance and review.

How does visual search work?

Images are embedded into vectors, stored in a vector database, and nearest vectors to a query image or text are retrieved and re-ranked with business rules.

How would you control the cost of multimodal features?

Use smaller models, cache results, batch processing, sample video frames, set budgets per request and monitor cost per outcome.

How do you handle consent for voice cloning?

Obtain explicit written consent, define scope and duration, secure samples, allow withdrawal, and prohibit impersonation.

Advanced AI PM · 17 classes · basic to advanced

System Design & Databases for PMs

System design is how an app's parts (screens, services, databases, payments, AI) work together so it stays fast, correct and affordable. PMs need it to ask the right questions, price trade-offs and explain decisions.

Download the PDFCourse pageAsk the AI Tutor

Basic · Class 1

The big picture: what happens when you tap Buy

See every box on the whiteboard in plain words.

Imagine a quick-commerce app like Zepto or Blinkit. You open it, see milk, tap Buy. In about two seconds, a dozen systems cooperate. Here is each box, explained for a non-technical PM.

BoxPlain-words jobEveryday comparison
User / App UIThe screen you tap. It asks the service for data and shows the answer.The shop counter
GeolocationFinds where you are and which nearby store can deliver.Google Maps on the counter
Service (API)The brain with the business rules: check stock, price, create the order. Many small services is called microservices.The shop manager
Inventory databaseStores how many items each store has. Read thousands of times a second.The stock register
Orders database (SQL)Stores orders, payments, refunds exactly and safely.The cash book
PaymentTalks to UPI, cards and wallets through a gateway such as Razorpay.The card machine
Vendor appThe store or seller updates stock and prices and accepts orders.The shopkeeper's phone
Chatbot + customer supportAnswers "where is my order?" and hands tough cases to humans.The help desk
Vector databaseLets AI search by meaning, so the chatbot finds the right help article.A librarian who understands what you mean
Consensus nodes (Paxos / Raft)A few servers that must agree on one truth, even if one fails.Four partners who must agree on the same ledger
Your job as a PM is not to draw this perfectly. It is to ask the right "what happens when…" questions: when two people buy the last item, when payment fails after stock is taken, when a server dies on sale day.
Key takeaways
  • Every tap triggers many systems working together.
  • Each box has one job; failures happen between boxes.
  • You do not build it, but you must be able to question it.
Practice: Draw your favourite app's Buy flow with 8 boxes and write one 'what if this fails?' question for each arrow.
Basic · Class 2

Why PMs need this: the business view

Connect technical choices to money, trust and speed.

System design looks technical, but every choice is a business trade-off. Engineers decide how; PMs decide what matters most. Without that, teams over-build or under-protect.

Business goalTechnical leverPM decision
More salesFast pages and search (caching, indexes, CDN)What is our target load time on a 4G phone?
Customer trustNo double charge, no oversold stock (transactions, idempotency)Which actions must never be wrong, even if slower?
Sale-day survivalScaling, queues, replicas, load testsWhat traffic do we plan for, 5x or 20x?
Lower cost per orderRight database for each job, storage tiersWhat can we afford per 1,000 orders?
Legal safetyEncryption, data location, access control (DPDP Act, RBI rules, PCI-DSS)Which data is sensitive, and who may see it?
Fast shipping of featuresClear services and APIsWhich team owns which part?

Numbers PMs should know

  • Latency: time for one request. Watch p95/p99 (the slow 5% or 1% of users), not only the average.
  • Availability: 99.9% allows about 8.8 hours of downtime a year; 99.99% only about 53 minutes.
  • SLA / SLO / SLI: the promise to customers / the internal target / the measured number.
  • RPO / RTO: how much data you can lose / how long you can be down after a disaster.
A cheap rule: spend reliability budget where mistakes cost real money or trust (payments, stock, personal data) and accept simpler, cheaper setups where a small error is harmless (likes, view counts).
Key takeaways
  • Technical choices are business trade-offs.
  • Protect money, stock and personal data first.
  • Ask for p95/p99 and availability targets in every spec.
Practice: Pick a feature you own. List the one thing that must never be wrong and the one thing that can be a little stale.
Basic · Class 3

SQL databases in plain words

Understand tables, keys, joins and indexes without code fear.

A SQL (relational) database is a set of tables, like linked Excel sheets. Each row is a record; keys link rows across tables. SQL is the language to ask questions. Examples: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle.

TableColumns
productsproduct_id (key), name, price
inventorystore_id, product_id, qty, state
ordersorder_id (key), user_id, store_id, total, status
-- How many packets of milk are available in store 7?
SELECT qty FROM inventory
WHERE store_id = 7 AND product_id = 42 AND state = 'available';
  • Primary key: the unique ID of a row. Foreign key: a column pointing to another table's key.
  • Join: combine tables ("orders with the customer's name").
  • Index: a lookup shortcut, like a book's index. Makes reads fast but writes a little slower and uses space.
  • Schema: the fixed structure of tables. Changing it needs a planned migration.
Choose SQL when data is structured, relationships matter, and correctness is critical: orders, payments, accounts, bookings, reports.
Key takeaways
  • SQL = tables with keys, queried by joins.
  • Indexes trade write speed for read speed.
  • Default to SQL for money and orders.
Practice: Sketch three tables for a food-delivery app and mark the primary and foreign keys.
Basic · Class 4

ACID: why money and stock stay correct

Learn the four promises of a database transaction.

A transaction groups steps so they succeed or fail together. Example: buying the last milk packet means (1) reduce stock, (2) create the order, (3) record the payment. If step 3 fails, steps 1 and 2 must undo.

LetterPromisePlain example
AtomicityAll steps happen or none doMoney leaves your account only if it reaches the shop
ConsistencyRules always holdStock never goes below zero
IsolationSimultaneous users do not corrupt each otherTwo buyers cannot both get the last item
DurabilityOnce confirmed, it survives a crashYour order still exists after a power cut
BEGIN;
UPDATE inventory SET qty = qty - 1
  WHERE store_id = 7 AND product_id = 42 AND qty > 0;
INSERT INTO orders (user_id, store_id, status) VALUES (101, 7, 'created');
COMMIT;   -- or ROLLBACK if anything failed
Transactions are why SQL databases are trusted for payments. Many NoSQL databases trade some of these promises for speed and scale, which is the key trade-off in the next classes.
Key takeaways
  • Transaction = all-or-nothing group of steps.
  • ACID protects money and stock.
  • Isolation is the promise behind 'no double selling'.
Practice: Write the steps of a UPI payment and mark which must be all-or-nothing.
Intermediate · Class 5

NoSQL: the main types and when to use them

Pick between key-value, document, wide-column and graph stores.

NoSQL means "not only SQL": databases that skip fixed tables and joins to scale across many servers and handle flexible data. They usually relax some ACID promises for speed (see BASE in class 7).

TypeShapeGood forExamples
Key-valueOne key → one valueSessions, carts, caches, counters, feature flagsRedis, DynamoDB
DocumentJSON-like documentsProduct catalogue, user profiles with varied fieldsMongoDB, Firestore
Wide-columnRows grouped by a partition key, huge and sparseMessages, activity feeds, time-series, IoT, write-heavy dataCassandra, ScyllaDB, HBase
GraphNodes and relationshipsFriends, fraud rings, recommendationsNeo4j, Neptune
VectorNumbers that capture meaningAI search and chatbots (class 14)Pinecone, pgvector, Qdrant

SQL vs NoSQL in one table

SQLNoSQL
StructureFixed tablesFlexible
RelationshipsJoins are easyUsually avoided or hand-built
ConsistencyStrong (ACID)Often eventual, tunable
ScalingVertical first, harder to spreadBuilt to spread across many servers
Best forOrders, payments, reportsHigh-volume reads/writes, flexible data
Common real-world answer: use both. SQL for orders and money, NoSQL (Redis/Cassandra/Mongo) for carts, catalogue, feeds and caches. This is called polyglot persistence.
Key takeaways
  • NoSQL has four main shapes plus vector.
  • It trades some consistency for scale and flexibility.
  • Most products use SQL and NoSQL together.
Practice: Match five data types in a food app (cart, orders, menu, chat, ratings) to a database type.
Intermediate · Class 6

Cassandra explained for PMs

Understand a masterless, always-on database.

Apache Cassandra is a wide-column NoSQL database built so there is no single point of failure. All servers (nodes) are equal and form a ring. It is popular where data arrives constantly and downtime is unacceptable: messages, activity feeds, order status events, sensor data.

  • Partition key: the field that decides which node stores a row (for example store_id). Chosen badly, one node gets overloaded (a "hot partition").
  • Replication factor (RF): how many copies exist. RF=3 means each row lives on three nodes.
  • Tunable consistency: per query you choose how many copies must answer. ONE = fastest, maybe stale; QUORUM = majority, safer; ALL = strongest, slowest.
  • Fast writes: it appends data first and tidies later (an LSM-tree design).
  • Query-first design: you design tables around the questions you will ask. Ad hoc queries and joins are weak.
StrengthsWeaknesses
Writes at massive scale, multi-region, survives node lossNo joins, limited ad hoc queries, transactions are limited and slow
Linear scale: add nodes to add capacityNeeds careful data modelling and operations skills

LWT (lightweight transactions) and the other terms you will hear

LWT is Cassandra's way to do a safe "check, then write" in one step, for example INSERT … IF NOT EXISTS (claim a username, create an order once) or UPDATE … IF qty > 0. Under the hood the replicas run a Paxos round (class 14) to agree, so it needs several network round trips: about 4 instead of 1. It is correct but much slower and gets worse when many people fight for the same row. Use it sparingly (claiming a unique ID, one-time actions), never on the hot path of every click.

INSERT INTO orders_by_key (idempotency_key, order_id, user_id)
VALUES ('chk-7f3a', 55, 101) IF NOT EXISTS;   -- LWT: only the first request wins
TermPlain meaning
CQLCassandra's SQL-like query language
Partition key / clustering keyPartition key decides which node; clustering key decides the order of rows inside that partition (for example newest first)
Consistency levelsONE (fast), QUORUM (majority), LOCAL_QUORUM (majority inside one data centre, the usual choice for multi-region), ALL (every copy), SERIAL (used by LWT)
GossipNodes chat with each other to learn who is up or down; no central boss
Commit log + memtable + SSTableA write goes to a safety log and to memory first, then is flushed to immutable files on disk (SSTables). This is why writes are fast
CompactionBackground merging of SSTables to keep reads fast and reclaim space
TombstoneA delete marker. Many tombstones slow reads, so avoid patterns that delete constantly (queues in a table)
TTLTime to live: rows that expire automatically (OTPs, sessions, 8-minute stock holds)
Hinted handoff, read repair, anti-entropy repairThe ways copies that missed a write catch up, so replicas converge (eventual consistency)
Replication strategy / data centreNetworkTopologyStrategy places copies across racks and regions; this is how Cassandra survives a whole data centre going down
VnodesEach server owns many small slices of the ring so data spreads evenly and new nodes take load smoothly
DenormalisationStore the same data in several tables, one per query, because there are no joins
PM question: "Do we need always-on writes at huge scale, or do we need strict transactions?" If the answer is strict transactions (payments, stock decrement), choose SQL or a database with strong transactions instead.
Key takeaways
  • Cassandra = equal nodes in a ring, data copied several times.
  • You choose consistency per query.
  • Great for high-volume writes, poor for joins and strict transactions.
  • LWT adds safe check-then-write using Paxos, but is slow: use it sparingly.
Practice: List three features in a delivery app that fit Cassandra (hint: tracking pings, chat, event logs) and one that does not.
Intermediate · Class 7

Scaling data: replication, sharding, caching, CAP and BASE

Know how products stay fast and available as they grow.

TechniquePlain meaningTrade-off
ReplicationKeep copies on several servers for safety and read speedCopies can lag (stale reads)
Sharding / partitioningSplit data by a key (city, store, user id range) across serversCross-shard queries and transactions are harder
CachingKeep popular answers in memoryMust expire or refresh, or users see old data
IndexingPre-built lookupsMore storage, slower writes
Load balancerSpreads requests across many serversNeeds health checks
CDNServes images and files from nearby serversCache invalidation

CAP theorem in one minute

When a network splits and servers cannot talk to each other, a system must choose between Consistency (everyone sees the same truth, so some requests are refused) and Availability (always answer, maybe with stale data). Partition tolerance is not optional on a real network.

Choose consistency (CP)Choose availability (AP)
Payments, final stock decrement, seat bookingProduct browsing, recommendations, view counts, "30 people watching"

BASE is the NoSQL counterpart of ACID: Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent. "Eventually" means copies agree after a short delay, often milliseconds.

Quorum rule: with N copies, if reads (R) and writes (W) each touch enough copies so that R + W > N, a read always sees the latest write. Example: N=3, R=2, W=2.
Key takeaways
  • Replication, sharding, caching and indexing are the four scaling tools.
  • CAP: during a network split you cannot have both perfect consistency and perfect availability.
  • Use strong consistency only where wrong data costs money or trust.
Practice: Classify ten features of a shopping app as 'must be exact' or 'can be a bit stale'.
Intermediate · Class 8

Services and servers: what happens when volume grows

Follow the app from 100 users to 10 million without the jargon.

A server is a computer running your code. A service is one job done by that code (catalogue, orders, payments). As more people use the app, you do not need smarter code first; you need more copies of the same code and a database layer that can keep up.

TrafficWhat the team doesPM impact
1x: launch dayOne server and one database are enough. Keep it simple.Ship features fast
5xAdd a load balancer and several identical servers; add a cache for hot data; add a read replica.Page speed stays steady
20x: a sale or festivalAutoscaling adds servers on demand; queues take slow work (emails, invoices) off the checkout path; rate limits protect the system.Plan promotions with engineering; pre-warm for known peaks
100x: a national appShard the database by city or user; split into microservices; use several regions; add a CDN for images.Cost and team ownership become the main questions

The key ideas

  • Vertical scaling = a bigger machine (simple, has a ceiling). Horizontal scaling = more machines (no ceiling, needs the design below).
  • Stateless services: a server keeps no customer data in its own memory, so any server can answer any request and one can fail without anyone noticing. State lives in the database, cache or session store.
  • Autoscaling: rules like "add a server when CPU is above 60%". It takes a minute or two, so it cannot catch a sudden 50x spike; prepare ahead.
  • Containers and Kubernetes: packaging code so identical copies start fast and are managed automatically.
  • Queues and backpressure: when work arrives faster than it can be done, put it in line instead of crashing; slow down or reject extra requests politely (HTTP 429).
  • Graceful degradation: when overloaded, switch off the non-essential (recommendations, live counters) to protect checkout.
  • Bottlenecks move: after servers, the database is next; after the database, a third-party API such as the payment gateway. Find the weakest link with a load test.
  • Circuit breakers and load shedding: stop calling a failing dependency so one problem does not become a full outage.
Sale-day checklist for a PM: expected peak orders per second, load test passed at 2x that, autoscaling limits raised, cache warmed, payment gateway limits confirmed in writing, feature flags ready to switch off extras, on-call named, rollback plan.
Key takeaways
  • Scale by adding identical stateless servers behind a load balancer.
  • Protect the database with caches, replicas and queues.
  • Find the next bottleneck with load tests before the sale, not during it.
Practice: Write a sale-day plan for a 20x traffic spike: what scales, what is switched off, and who is on call.
Intermediate · Class 9

The inventory problem: never sell the last item twice

Walk the whiteboard's qty = 1 problem and its fixes.

Two customers see "1 left" and tap Buy at the same moment. If both read qty = 1 and both subtract, you sell two and have one. This is a race condition. The fix is to make the check and the subtraction one indivisible step.

ApproachHow it worksGood for
Atomic updateUPDATE … SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE qty > 0; if 0 rows changed, it is sold outSimple, most cases
Pessimistic lockLock the row while one buyer decidesRare, very hot items; can slow everyone
Optimistic lockRead a version number; update only if it has not changed; else retryMany readers, fewer conflicting buyers
Reservation (hold)Reserve the item for 5-10 minutes during checkout, then confirm or releaseTickets, tatkal seats, flash sales
Queue per itemPut buyers in line and process one by oneExtreme flash sales

Other rules that protect money

  • Idempotency key: a unique request ID so a retried tap or a repeated payment callback does not create a second order or second charge.
  • Two-phase commit (2PC): several systems agree to commit together; strong but slow and fragile.
  • Saga: a chain of steps, each with an undo ("refund", "release stock"). Popular in microservices.
  • Outbox pattern: write the order and the "order created" event together, then publish the event, so none gets lost.
Product choices: how long is a hold (stock locked vs lost sales)? Do we show "only 2 left" (real-time cost vs urgency)? What do we do when payment fails after stock is held (auto-release, notify)?
Key takeaways
  • The last-item problem is a race; fix it with one atomic step.
  • Holds with a timeout balance sales and fairness.
  • Idempotency keys stop double orders and double charges.
Practice: Define hold time, release rule and message for a 'last seat' booking feature.
Intermediate · Class 10

The full user journey: every step, system and risk

Follow one order from opening the app to delivery and refunds.

#What the user doesSystems involvedDataWhat can go wrong, and the protection
1Opens the app, logs in with OTP, shares locationAuth service, SMS provider, geolocationUser profile (SQL), session (Redis)OTP abuse (rate limit); duplicate accounts (unique verified phone); location consent
2Sees the nearest store and productsGeo service, catalogue, search, vector search, cache, CDNCatalogue (document store), stock snapshot (cache)Stale stock (label as approximate); slow load (cache, CDN)
3Adds items to the cartCart service, inventory serviceCart (key-value store), soft hold on stockCart lost (persist per user); hold never released (TTL)
4Chooses address and slot, sees the totalAddress, pricing, offers, tax servicesAddresses and coupons (SQL)Price changes mid-checkout (price lock per cart version); coupon abused (one use per user)
5Taps PayOrder service, payment gateway (UPI, cards, wallets)Order (SQL) in status PENDING, payment recordDouble tap or retry (idempotency); money taken but no order (reconciliation)
6Sees "Order confirmed"Webhook handler, order and inventory services, notificationsOrder PAID, stock deductedLate or repeated webhooks (dedupe by payment id); stock gone (auto refund)
7Tracks the orderVendor app, picker app, rider app, maps, event streamStatus events and rider pings (wide-column / stream)Missed updates (event replay); wrong ETA (re-estimate)
8Delivered; rates, returns or asks for helpSupport, chatbot with vector search, refund serviceTickets and refunds (SQL), help articles (vector DB)Refund repeated (refund idempotency); bot gives a wrong answer (guardrails, human handover)

Journey metrics a PM watches

  • Funnel: browse, cart, checkout started, payment attempted, payment succeeded, delivered. Each drop has a cause: speed, trust, price, payment failure.
  • Payment success rate (by method and bank), order success rate, p95 checkout time, cancellation and refund rate, duplicate order rate (target zero).
  • Support contacts per 100 orders as a quality signal for the whole chain.
Order states (a simple state machine): CREATED, PAYMENT_PENDING, PAID, PACKED, OUT_FOR_DELIVERY, DELIVERED, with side exits CANCELLED, FAILED and REFUNDED. Only allowed moves are accepted, which is what makes repeated or out-of-order messages harmless.
Key takeaways
  • Every journey step touches different systems and data stores.
  • Each step has a named risk and a named protection.
  • An order state machine keeps messy real life under control.
Practice: Map your own app's journey in the same table and add the metric you would track at each step.
Advanced · Class 11

Payment checkout in detail

Understand how a payment really moves, and why it is asynchronous.

Payments are asynchronous: your app starts a payment, the user finishes it in another app (UPI, bank page), and the gateway tells you the result later. The screen result can be wrong or lost, so the server-to-server confirmation is the truth.

  1. Create the order as PENDING in SQL with a unique idempotency key made when the user starts checkout. Price, items and address are frozen on the order.
  2. Create a payment with the gateway (Razorpay, PayU, Cashfree, Stripe, UPI intent). You get a payment id. Store it against the order.
  3. The user pays in the UPI app or card page. Your app only shows "waiting for payment".
  4. The gateway calls your webhook with the result. Verify the signature and that the amount and order id match. Never trust the client app's "success".
  5. Update in one transaction: mark the order PAID, convert the stock hold into a deduction, write a ledger entry.
  6. Publish an event (outbox) so notifications, warehouse and analytics follow.
  7. Reconcile: a scheduled job compares your records with the gateway's settlement report and fixes mismatches (paid but no order, order but no payment).
Payment stateMeaningWhat the app does
CREATEDPayment startedWait; show a countdown
PENDINGBank or UPI has not confirmedPoll the gateway; do not charge again
AUTHORISED / CAPTUREDMoney held / money takenConfirm the order after capture
FAILEDDeclined or timed outRelease stock, offer retry
REFUNDED / PARTIALMoney returnedUpdate the order; notify

Edge cases to ask about

  • Money debited but the app shows failure: keep the order PENDING until the gateway confirms; auto-refund after a defined window if the order cannot be fulfilled.
  • Webhook arrives twice, late or out of order: handlers must be idempotent and obey the state machine.
  • User closes the app mid-payment: the server still receives the webhook, so the order completes.
  • Gateway down: fail over to a second gateway or show clear messaging; do not lose the cart.
  • Cash on delivery: no gateway step, but the order still needs duplicate protection and fraud limits.
  • Security: never store raw card numbers (use gateway tokens, PCI-DSS); encrypt personal data; follow RBI rules and the DPDP Act.
Key takeaways
  • The server-side webhook, not the app screen, decides success.
  • Create the order first as PENDING, then confirm after verified payment.
  • Reconciliation catches whatever the real-time flow misses.
Practice: Draw the sequence of a UPI payment with five actors: user, app, your server, gateway, bank. Mark where a failure can occur.
Advanced · Class 12

Never twice: no repeated order, payment or customer

Use layered protections so duplicates cannot happen, even with retries.

Networks fail, users double tap, apps retry, and webhooks repeat. Systems normally guarantee at-least-once delivery (a message may arrive twice). True "exactly once" is built by combining at-least-once delivery with idempotent processing. You need protections at several layers because any single one can fail.

A. How to make sure an order is not repeated

  • Idempotency key: the app generates one key per checkout attempt (for example cart id plus cart version). Every retry sends the same key. The server stores key to order id. A second request with the same key returns the same order instead of making a new one.
  • Unique constraint in SQL: a unique index on (user_id, idempotency_key) means the database itself refuses a second row, even if the code has a bug or two servers race.
  • One active checkout per cart: a short lock (Redis SET key value NX EX 30, or a row lock) so two simultaneous taps on two servers cannot both proceed.
  • Order state machine: only legal moves are accepted, so a repeated "mark as paid" does nothing.
  • Time window rule: if the same user, store and basket is submitted twice within a few seconds, show "you already placed this order" with a link to it.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_order_idem ON orders (user_id, idempotency_key);

INSERT INTO orders (user_id, idempotency_key, status, total)
VALUES (101, 'chk-7f3a', 'PAYMENT_PENDING', 349)
ON CONFLICT (user_id, idempotency_key) DO NOTHING;   -- a repeat inserts nothing
SELECT order_id FROM orders WHERE user_id = 101 AND idempotency_key = 'chk-7f3a';

B. How to make sure a payment is not repeated

  • Send the gateway an idempotency key or a unique receipt reference per payment so a retried API call cannot create two charges.
  • Store the gateway payment id with a unique constraint; a webhook for an id already processed is acknowledged (HTTP 200) and ignored.
  • One order has at most one successful payment. If a second success arrives, auto-refund it and alert.
  • Refunds: an idempotency key per refund, and the refunded total never exceeds the paid total.
  • Reply quickly to a webhook and do heavy work asynchronously, so the gateway does not retry unnecessarily.

C. How to make sure no customer is repeated

  • Make the verified mobile number (and email, where used) unique, after normalising the format (+91, spaces, case).
  • Verify with an OTP before creating the account; use IDs from trusted logins (Google, Apple) as extra unique keys.
  • On signup, check then insert inside one transaction, backed by the unique index, so two simultaneous signups cannot both win.
  • Duplicate detection and merging: match on phone, email, device and name or address similarity; merge accounts with a documented process that moves orders, wallet and loyalty points and keeps an audit trail.
  • Abuse and promos: limit first-order offers per device, phone, payment instrument and address to stop repeat sign-ups.
  • Privacy: keep only needed identifiers, protect them, and honour deletion requests under the DPDP Act.
Where duplicates come fromFix
Double tap or slow screenDisable the button; idempotency key
Client retry after timeoutSame key returns the same order
Two servers handle one requestUnique database constraint; short lock
Webhook sent twiceDedupe by payment id; state machine
Queue redelivers a messageIdempotent consumer; processed-message table
Same person signs up twiceUnique verified phone; merge process
Test it: include duplicate scenarios in QA: double tap, kill the server mid-payment, replay the webhook five times, send the same signup from two phones. The target metric is zero duplicate orders and zero duplicate charges, tracked daily.
Key takeaways
  • Idempotency key plus a unique database constraint is the core defence.
  • Make every webhook and queue consumer idempotent.
  • Protect customers too: unique verified phone, OTP, merge process.
Practice: Write the duplicate-protection checklist for your product's checkout, signup and refund flows.
Advanced · Class 13

Consensus: Paxos and Raft without the maths

Understand why servers must agree and how they do it.

If four servers each keep a copy of the truth ("order 55 is paid"), what if two disagree? Consensus is how a group of servers agrees on one value even when some crash or messages are delayed. It is the engine behind reliable leaders, locks and configuration.

  • Paxos (Leslie Lamport): the classic algorithm. A proposer suggests a value, acceptors promise and accept, learners record the result. Two phases: prepare/promise, then accept. A value is chosen once a majority (quorum) accepts it.
  • Raft: designed to be easier to understand. One leader takes all writes and copies them to followers. If the leader dies, a new election starts.
  • Majority math: with N nodes you survive floor((N-1)/2) failures. 3 nodes tolerate 1, 5 nodes tolerate 2. The 4-node ring on the whiteboard tolerates only 1 (same as 3), which is why odd numbers are preferred.
Where you meet itWhat it protects
etcd (Raft), ZooKeeper (ZAB), ConsulCluster settings, leader election, distributed locks
Google Spanner (Paxos)Globally consistent database
Cassandra light-weight transactions"Insert only if not exists"
Kafka (KRaft)Keeping the message cluster's metadata consistent
What a PM should take away: consensus gives safety but costs speed. Every write needs a majority round-trip, so spreading across regions makes writes slower. You rarely build it; you choose products that already use it, and you accept the latency and cost that come with strong consistency.
Key takeaways
  • Consensus = servers agreeing on one value despite failures.
  • Majority (quorum) is the core idea; odd numbers of nodes are best.
  • Strong agreement costs latency, a trade-off PMs must price in.
Practice: Explain in three sentences to a friend why four partners must agree before a ledger entry is final.
Advanced · Class 14

Vector databases, geolocation and the AI parts

Add meaning search, location and chatbots to the design.

Vector databases

An embedding is a list of numbers that captures the meaning of text, an image or a product. Similar meanings sit close together. A vector database stores embeddings and finds the nearest ones quickly (ANN, approximate nearest neighbour, using methods like HNSW). So "something to have with chai" can find biscuits and rusks, even without those exact words.

UseExample
Semantic searchSearch that understands intent and Hinglish
RAG chatbotFind the right policy or help article, then let the AI answer from it
Recommendations"People who like this also like…"
Duplicate and fraud detectionNear-identical listings or reviews
  • Hybrid search: combine keywords (BM25) with vectors, and add filters such as city, in stock, price.
  • Options: a vector DB (Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus) or the pgvector add-on to Postgres, often enough for starting out.
  • Watch: re-embedding cost when content changes, relevance testing (evals), and privacy of what you embed.
  • Not for: exact lookups like "order 55". Use SQL for those.

Geolocation

  • Store places as latitude and longitude; use geohash or Uber's H3 hex grid to group nearby points fast.
  • Tools: PostGIS (Postgres), Redis GEO, Elasticsearch geo queries, Google Maps APIs.
  • Typical questions: which dark store is within 2 km and has stock? What is the ETA? Is this pin inside the service area?
  • Privacy: ask consent, collect only what you need, follow the DPDP Act.
AI and location features are additions to the same architecture: they read from the inventory and orders data, they do not replace the SQL ledger.
Key takeaways
  • Vector DBs search by meaning, not exact words.
  • RAG uses a vector DB to ground chatbot answers.
  • Geohash and H3 make 'nearest store' fast.
Practice: Design the vector-search and location steps for 'find me a 10-minute dinner nearby'.
Advanced · Class 15

The supporting cast: APIs, queues, events and observability

Know the other terms that appear in every design review.

TermPlain meaningWhy a PM cares
API / REST / GraphQLThe doors through which apps and partners talk to your serviceContract with partners; versioning breaks apps
Monolith vs microservicesOne big app vs many small servicesSpeed of teams vs operational complexity
Message queue (Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS)A line where work waits to be processed laterHandles spikes, avoids blocking the user
Event-driven / pub-subServices announce "order created" and others reactLoose coupling, but harder to trace
WebhookA partner calls your URL when something happensPayment status updates; needs retries and idempotency
Rate limiting / backoffCap requests; wait longer between retriesPrevents abuse and retry storms
Circuit breakerStop calling a failing service for a whileOne failure does not take everything down
OLTP vs OLAPLive transactions vs analytics and reportingDo not run heavy reports on the live database
CDCChange data capture: stream database changes elsewhereFeeds search, analytics and caches
Feature flags / canary / blue-greenRelease to a few users or switch between two versionsSafe rollouts and quick rollback
ObservabilityLogs, metrics and traces to see what is happeningFaster incident response; ask for dashboards in specs

Back-of-the-envelope sizing (a PM skill)

1 million orders a day is about 12 orders per second on average (1,000,000 / 86,400). Plan for peaks of 10x, so about 120 per second. If each order takes 2 KB, that is about 2 GB a day or roughly 730 GB a year. Browsing is far larger than buying: expect 50 to 100 reads for every order, so cache hot data.

Ask engineers: "What is our peak requests per second, our p99 latency, and what breaks first if traffic doubles?"
Key takeaways
  • Know the vocabulary: API, queue, event, webhook, cache, observability.
  • Queues and events absorb spikes but add complexity.
  • Estimate scale with simple arithmetic before debating tools.
Practice: Estimate requests per second and daily storage for an app with 200,000 orders a day.
Advanced · Class 16

Case study and PM interview answer: design inventory and checkout

Practise a complete answer from requirements to trade-offs.

Prompt: "Design inventory and checkout for a 10-minute grocery delivery app."

  1. Clarify: users, cities, stores, items per store, flash sales? Out of scope: delivery routing.
  2. Goals and metrics: no overselling, checkout under 2 seconds p95, 99.95% availability, order success rate, refund rate.
  3. Scale: 1M orders/day, peak 10x, 100 reads per order.
  4. High-level design: app, API gateway, services (catalogue, inventory, order, payment, notifications), SQL for orders, key-value/Redis for carts and stock cache, Kafka for events, vector DB for support search, geolocation for the nearest store.
  5. Deep dive (inventory): per-store stock in a fast store, atomic decrement, 8-minute holds, release on timeout, reconcile with the vendor app hourly.
  6. Failure modes: payment succeeds but order write fails (saga plus idempotency), a node dies (replicas, quorum), vendor app offline (last-known stock, safety buffer).
  7. Trade-offs: consistency for stock and money, availability for browsing, cost of real-time counts.
  8. Rollout: pilot in one city, feature flags, dashboards, alerts, rollback plan.
Interviewers rewardInterviewers penalise
Clarifying questions, metrics, trade-offs, user impact, simple numbersTool name-dropping, no numbers, ignoring failure cases, over-engineering
One-line answer: "Strong consistency for stock and payments, eventual consistency for browsing, holds to protect the last item, idempotency to survive retries, and metrics to prove it works."
Key takeaways
  • Answer in a fixed order: clarify, metrics, scale, design, deep dive, failures, trade-offs, rollout.
  • Name the hard part and solve it.
  • Tie every choice to a user or business outcome.
Practice: Record yourself giving this answer in 5 minutes using the eight steps.
Advanced · Class 17

Final project: write a one-page system brief

Produce a PM-friendly design brief you can share with engineers.

Choose a product (food delivery, ticket booking, wallet, ed-tech) and write a one-page brief that answers:

  • What are the 5 core data types and which database fits each (SQL, key-value, document, wide-column, vector)?
  • Which operations must be strongly consistent, and which can be eventually consistent?
  • How do you prevent double selling or double charging?
  • What scale and latency targets do you assume, and how did you estimate them?
  • What are the top 3 failure scenarios and your response?
  • What does it cost per 1,000 orders, and what is the lever to reduce it?

Share it with an engineer and ask for the three biggest risks they see. Update the brief with their answers.

Key takeaways
  • A good brief is short, numeric and honest about trade-offs.
  • Engineers improve a draft faster than a blank page.
  • Keep the brief updated as the product scales.
Practice: Complete the one-page system brief and review it with an engineer.
Toolkit

Cheat sheet

SQLTables with fixed structure, joins and strong guarantees
NoSQLFlexible, scalable stores (key-value, document, wide-column, graph)
ACIDAtomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability: safe transactions
BASEBasically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent
CAPIn a network split choose consistency or availability
CassandraMasterless wide-column database for huge write volumes
Paxos / RaftAlgorithms that make servers agree on one value using a majority
QuorumA majority of copies; R + W > N gives fresh reads
Vector DBStores embeddings and finds similar meaning fast
ReplicationCopies of data on several servers
ShardingSplitting data across servers by a key
CacheHot data kept in memory (Redis)
Idempotency keyMakes retries safe
SagaA chain of steps with undo actions
2PCTwo-phase commit across systems
Hold / reservationTemporary stock lock during checkout
p95 / p99Latency of the slower 5% / 1% of requests
SLA / SLO / SLIPromise / target / measurement
Geohash / H3Grid systems for fast location lookup
RAGAI answers grounded in retrieved documents
LWTCassandra lightweight transaction: IF NOT EXISTS / IF condition, slow because it uses Paxos
IdempotentRepeating gives the same result as doing it once
Stateless serviceKeeps no customer data in server memory, so copies can be added freely
AutoscalingAdding or removing servers automatically with load
ReconciliationComparing your records with the gateway or bank and fixing mismatches
Interview prep

20 interview questions with answers

Why do PMs need to know SQL vs NoSQL?

Because the choice affects consistency, cost, speed and features. PMs should know SQL is best for money and orders, NoSQL for scale and flexibility, and most products use both.

Explain ACID to a non-technical person.

It is four promises that make a transaction safe: all-or-nothing, rules always hold, simultaneous users do not interfere, and confirmed data survives a crash.

What is the CAP theorem?

In a network split a system must pick between consistency (same truth everywhere, may refuse requests) and availability (always answer, maybe stale). Pick consistency for payments, availability for browsing.

What is Cassandra good at?

Very high write volume, multi-region and always-on use cases like messages, feeds and event logs. It is weak at joins and strict transactions.

What is Paxos and why does it matter?

An algorithm that lets servers agree on one value using a majority, even with failures. It underpins reliable leaders, locks and strongly consistent databases, at the cost of some latency.

Paxos vs Raft?

Both achieve consensus. Raft is simpler to understand and implement, with a clear leader and elections; Paxos is the older, more general form.

How do you prevent selling the last item twice?

Make check and decrement one atomic step, use holds with timeouts, add idempotency keys, and reconcile stock with vendors.

What is idempotency and why for payments?

Repeating a request has the same effect as doing it once. It stops double charges when users retry or a payment callback arrives twice.

When would you use a vector database?

For meaning-based search, RAG chatbots, recommendations and near-duplicate detection. Not for exact lookups.

What is RAG?

Retrieval-augmented generation: fetch relevant documents (often via a vector DB) and let the AI answer using them, which reduces made-up answers.

Replication vs sharding?

Replication copies the same data for safety and read speed; sharding splits different data across servers for capacity.

How would you estimate load for 1M orders a day?

About 12 per second on average, 120 per second at a 10x peak, 2 GB of order data a day, and many more reads than writes.

What would you ask engineers before a sale?

Expected peak requests per second, p99 latency, what fails first, load-test results, rollback plan and on-call coverage.

Monolith or microservices?

Start simple; split services when teams and scale require it. Microservices bring speed for teams but add network, data and debugging complexity.

What is a Cassandra LWT?

A lightweight transaction (IF NOT EXISTS or IF condition) that runs a Paxos round for a safe check-then-write. It is correct but slow, so use it only for rare, important actions like claiming a unique key.

What happens when traffic grows 20x?

Add a load balancer and many identical stateless servers with autoscaling, cache hot data, add read replicas, move slow work to queues, rate limit, and switch off non-essentials. The next bottleneck is usually the database or a third-party API.

How do you stop duplicate orders?

Use an idempotency key per checkout attempt, a unique database constraint on it, a short lock per cart, an order state machine and a disabled button. Replays return the same order.

Why is payment confirmed by webhook?

The user may close the app or the screen may be wrong. The gateway tells your server the verified result, so the server decides, and reconciliation fixes any mismatch.

How do you avoid duplicate customers?

A unique, normalised, OTP-verified phone number backed by a database constraint, a transactional check-then-insert, a documented merge process and promo limits.

What is a saga?

A series of local transactions with compensating undo steps (refund, release stock) used instead of one giant distributed transaction.

Product Design for PMs: Complete Guide

Product design is deciding how a product works and feels so real people can solve a real problem easily. PMs do not draw screens; they own the problem, the users and the outcomes, and they work with designers to get there.
